Hon. SYDNEY FISHER moved second reading of Bill (No. 193) to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
Will the hon. minister be good enough to explain the purport of the Bill?

When I moved the resolution on which this Bill is based, I explained that the amendments are almost entirely of a verbal character. There is no change of principle at all, and the amendments would be better considered as they are detailed when we are in Committee going over the Bill clause by clause. They are due to some little difficulties which have arisen in the administration of the Act.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1, interpretation.

The only change in the first subclause is to add the word ' game ' tc the list of animals. The next subclause in the Act as it stands at present reads:
' Export' means export out of Canada or out of a province in which the establishment is situated to another province.
The Act applies to some goods which have never been in what is technically called an establishment. The word ' establishment' is not necessary in the administration of the Act. We therefore propose to leave out the words defining an establishment. The next subclause is a new' one and defines a farmer. The Act permits the slaughter and sale of animals by farmers without inspection, and w'e have found some difficulty in defining clearly what a farmer is. \\ e therefore insert this definition:
A farmer is a person whose recognized occupation is that of farming, and who slaughters only such animals as are fed bv him on his own premises.
Some dealers have been claiming to be farmers, and we wish to define distinctly those who have the privilege allowed to farmers under the Act.
Will this definition take in the Minister of Agriculture?	.
I think so.

Will the minister explain why he uses the wmrd ' goats ' in this Sir WILFRID LAURIER: ~
Bill? Is it intended to can goats as food, or what is the object? 1 am afraid this would open the door a long way for adulterated foods. Some people make cheese out of goat's milk, but I am not aware that they have come dowrn to eating goats. I think the minister ought to explain why he is giving the men who are running these canning factories an opportunity of palming off goat's meat instead of other meat which the people usually eat. Perhaps the minister could explain whether he intends this goat meat for export or for local consumption. So far as Ontario is concerned, he need not bother about it, because we have not vet got dowm to eating goats or horses either. But at the same time I do not think we should send from Canada to the old country canned goats. Surely the minister has made a mistake.
In the first place, this is not an amendment because the word ' goats ' appears in the original Act.
Why not take it out?

It could be taken out. I do not think there is any quantity of goat [DOT]meat used in Canada, but there is a good deal of it slaughtered in the United States and it might be shipped in here. This clause simply enables us to deal with that if it should be sent into our market. I know, as does m.y hon. friend, that goat meat is not used in Ontario or in Canada at all for that matter, but it might be imported, and, as is well known, there are ai number of flocks of goats being encouraged in the country for other purposes, and as some of them might be slaughtered and put upon the market we could not deal with such a case unless this word were in the clause.
Is there anything in this Bill or in the original Act w'hich prohibits those engaged in the canning industry from canning goat meat?
Not so long as they cal! it goat meat.

This Bill defines a farmer as a person whose recognized occupation is that of farming. There are many people in Canada wdiose recognized occupation may not be farming, but who, nevertheless, are carrying on farming extensively, and who if under this Act they were deprived of any rights which a farmer might enjoy, would be treated unjustly.

I think, subject to correction, that if a man was running a farm in any way this clause wrould include him. For instance, my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is a doctor, and if he ran a farm as well I think he would be recognized as engaged in the occupation of farming. I would not wish to restrict the interpretation in that

sense, and there is no such intention in the drafting of the clause.

This Bill applies to food, that is exported, but so far as the Canadian consumers are concerned any kind of diseased animals may be sold to them. I saw a case in Toronto not long ago where diseased meat was sold for 11 cents per pound for the purpose of canning it, and the vendor was brought before the magistrate and fined $20. Then, calves only a few days old are put on the Canadian market. As I understand it, the Minister of Agriculture is using all his efforts to see that the good meat goes to a foreign country and that the refuse is left in Canada. The minister has promised session after session to provide a remedy, but he is not doing so in this Bill.

Aly hon. friend is bringing up the old, old question which has been discussed time and again in this House. The question of local slaughtering and of protecting the health of the people is a provincial matter and it is only the export and interprovincial trade that this Bill professes to deal with. The case which my hon. friend mentioned is a local matter and we have nothing to do with it. I have no hesitation in saying that while we might have the power, it would be inadvisable and impracticable for Dominion officials to interfere in such matters. If we attempted to do so we would very soon have a most violent protest from the provincial and municipal authorities.
The minister does not think it would be unconstitutional for us to do it?
It may be that we could constitutionally do it, but it is inadvisable.
And the minister now says he refuses to do anything to protect the health of the people of this country?

That is not a correct definition of what I said.
Mr. 3. D. REID. Then make it plain.

I said that so far as the making of local arrangements are concerned these are in the hands of provincial and municipal authorities and that it was not for us to interfere with them in that work. As to export trade and interprovincial trade, this Act deals with that and we have been trying to enforce it.
The minister is not dealing with municipal matters in this Act.
That is just what I said.
It is the first time in the history of the minister that he has been anxious not to put on more government officials and to exercise patronage.
Oh, no, quite the contrary.
Every time he has a chance he has been creating new officials.
My hon. friend knows better.
I don't think there is a member in this House who would dispute that fact.
Yes, there are.

The minister in this case is willing to appoint officials to protect the health of the people of foreign countries, but he will not appoint inspectors to safeguard the health of our own people. I think that is an awful condition for a minister to be m who has charge of the Agricultural Department, and is supposed to do something for the farmers. I cannot see yet where we have ever had any benefit from the department. Here is a chance now where he can protect both tlid farmers and the community if he would put on a horde of officials and see that we get decent meat to eat. The Prime Minister knows that we ought to have pure food in Canada. [DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And more patronage.

If it is necessary to have more patronage in order that we may have pure meat, I am willing to have more patronage. But the Prime Minister agrees with me that we should have pure meat, and yet his Alinister of Agriculture sitting beside him, absolutely refuses to give it. The result is that if the policy of the Alinister of Agriculture is carried out, we will have rotten meat to eat. Now, I think the Prime Alinister is just as guilty as his Minister of Agriculture, because, while he is trying to get all the patronage he can, he does nothing to compel his minister to give us pure meat. It is a notorious fact that the Alinister of Agriculture has always been guilty of putting on officials wherever he can possibly do it; but in this particular case where more officials are necessary to protect the health and lives of people, he refuses to put them on.

Aly hon. friend in one part of his address exactly contradicts what he says in another part. He abuses me foxasking for more patronage, and then he abuses me because I won't take it. Here is an evidence that I do not want patronage. I may say to my hon. friend that none are so blind as those who do not wish to see. He cannot see anything good in the Department of Agriculture.

I may mention one thing that the minister did do on behalf of this country. He undertook to show the people how they could make a profit out of



hens. Now he has got 323 hens out there, and he pays $4,500 a year for looking after them. He has a general superintendent that he pays $1,500; then he has a foreman that he pays $1,000; then he has a man to cary water to these liens, and he pays $800 to him; then lie has another man to feed the hens, and pays him $800; then he has another man to clean up the hen house, and pays him $600. So altogether lie pays $4,500 a year for looking after these 323 hens, and all the return he gets out of them is $350. There is something that lie is doing for the farmers of this country, and there is also a glaring case'of patronage. But now that he has a chance to do something to give the people pure food, the Minister of Agriculture stands up here and absolutely refuses to protect the lives of the public, and probably the lives of their children, by allowing them to continue to eat this diseased meat.

The logical sequence of the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture is this, that so far as interprovincial trade is concerned, he has jurisdiction now. I would like to ask him if he is exercising that jurisdiction in regard to provincial trade. This question has also arisen in the United States, where one of the great industries is that of slaughtering cattle for meat. It has concentrated itself in the great centres of the United States like Chicago and Kansas City. They have now a federal act for the inspection of meat largely used for domestic purposes, even when it is not exported but is sent into other states. Now that thing must come in Canada. The slaughter of the meat supply of Canada will be done largely in some centre like Winnipeg, and is being largely done in the city of Toronto to-day. There is a great interprovincial trade originating in those centres, so the minister will have to take jurisdiction more or less in this matter, and exercise official supervision of meats for the interprovincial trade. He is seized of that authority now. I wish to know now if he is enforcing the law as regards the product of abattoirs in our present meat killing centres, when that product is sent into other provinces.

Yes. Every establishment which does any interprovincial or export trade has in it an inspector of the Department of Agriculture, whose business it is to supervise and watch the animals when they come in, their slaughter and their preparation for food. We do not touch abattoirs or slaughter houses which are purely local in their character, leaving that to provincial or municipal authorities. Imnorters are also subject to this Act.
In about how many meat killing centres now is this jurisdiction asserted?
About 40 establishments are under inspection in various parts of the country, including these large ones in Toronto.	[DOT]

I quite agree with any effort that is made on the part of the Department of Agriculture to ensure that the public shall get pure and healthy meat, for consumption. One objection to the inspection made by the department, is that, while in the large cities there are inspectors of abattoirs where the meat is exported or liable to be exported, the bulk of the meat that enters into local consumption in cities and towns is not subject to any inspection at all. As a consequence, animals that are liable to be diseased in any way are overlooked. The owners of these animals sell them to the small butchers and they are consumed all over the country as human food, while the best of the meat is nearly all shipped out of the country. On this occasion I would like also to voice a complaint and bring it to the attention of the minister to see if some method cannot be adopted to secure a more equitable distribution of the loss and expense of inspection. It is manifestly in the interest of the public that meat should be inspected, but the expense and loss incurred in that connection is not borne equitably by the public. There are over 400 drovers in the province of Ontario. Those 400 men purchase their cattle on the farm. The farmer sells a bullock to the butcher, the animal looks quite healthy, it goes to the stock yards, it there passes a visual inspection by an inspector who looks at it and passes it as a healthy animal. The drover purchases that animal on the condition that it passes inspection, and that is the inspection that it has to pass.
After it has passed the visual inspection from the car, it is sold to the packer or exporter, but the purchase is made from the drover on the distinct understanding that the animal must pass inspection as dead meat. But, when the animal is sent to the abattoir and slaughtered, it is discovered that it has had a touch of tuberculosis or some disease of that kind, and so the drover, having sold it subject to the inspection as dead meat, must lose every dollar that he paid for it. It may be said that he can go back to the farmer from whom he purchased it, but that is impossible, because the, animal wras not tagged to identify it as coming from any particular farmer. The result is that last year, in Ontario alone, the drovers lost over $400,000 from this inspection. For my part T quite believe that it is very proper that the department should conduct this inspection and proper that wre should make every effort to have wholesome meats; but I think also that a plan should be devised

whereby the party who loses this money should be compensated in some way. It is manifestly unfair that the man who lias purchased the animal in good faith from the farmer should lose, because after the animal has passed the visual inspection by the inspector, an official of this government, mind you-a defect which nobody has been able to discover and for which the drover is certainly not responsible, causes the condemnation .ol that carcass. The drovers of Ontario are seriously considering going out of business because they lost an average of about $1,000 each last year.
Do not the packing houses lose that?
Not a dollar; every cheque they give to the drovers is marked ' subject to inspection.'
In our locality, the pack' ing houses bear that loss.

The drovers, I understand, held a meeting in Toronto last week, when this grievance was talked over, and it was there shown that last year they had paid over $400,000 on this account. Now, this dead meat inspection is for the protection of the public, and it seems to me that the drovers ought to be compensated by some one for their loss. I thought that, as this matter was under discussion, I would call the .'attention of the minister to the point, because I do not think that, at heart, he is opposed to the view I take as a matter of justice. Every one knows that it is for the public good that this inspection occurs. Why, then, should these poor men be called on to pay the penalty for providing proper food for the whole community?- especially when you consider that most of this meat is exported, and so -our drovers are penalized in order to insure the purity and wholesomeness of {he food of foreign people. As I have said, there w'as over $400,000 worth of this meat condemned last year after having passed the general inspection at the yards where the cattle were unloaded from the car.
What became of the meat?

It was destroyed tanked. But the man who pays for it gets nothing for it. This matter should claim the attention of this House, and some means should be devised by the Department of Agriculture to remove this cause of hardship in the case of an important class of our citizens.

I am more anxious about the health of the people than about compensating anybody at the present time. I drew the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to this question of diseased meat a year ago. I told him that 2001
j 1 _ knew of a number of animals affected ; with tuberculosis being butchered and sold to the people of this country. And I tell him that now. If he wants to take the matter up-and I wish he would-I will prove my statement by the men who are buying these cattle and who are ready to come here to Ottawa and give their testimony on the subject.

My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Owen) makes a statement which I do not dispute. I know that many animals are slaughtered that are not in perfectly sound health, and, no doubt, the meat is sold in many cases for human consumption. That is not the case in any abattoir ot meat packing house under the operation of this Act. If the municipal councils and the provincial authorities do not choose to prevent what the hon. gentleman has mentined in the slaughter houses under their control, I am sorry for them, but I am not responsible. If these slaughter-houses were under the operation of this Act for export lor interprovincial trade, what my hon. friend has stated could not occur.
I may say to my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) that this question of the difficulties of the drovers, packers and farmers, as to who is responsible for the losses to which he has referred, is a very complex one, but one which I consider to be more -a matter of trade arrangement amongst the parties concerned in the business than for governmental interference. I know that statements are made such as my hon. friend has made here today. We had a deputation of the packers and men representing these packing establishments for which these drovers buy, and these gentlemen said that the . loss fell on the packing-houses.
That is not so now.

I am not saying which of these statements is right; I am only stating what these gentlemen said. The hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Sealeyl has just stated that the packing houses in Hamilton suffer this loss. In any case, it seems to me that it is properly a matter of commercial arrangement among the parties interested. I do not see how the government could step in and undertake to bear the loss in regard to these dead animals. For it is to be observed that the loss does not occur until the animal is made into meat. Under the Contagious Diseases of Animals Act, which has to do with living animals, we do certain work and pay certain compensation, for the reason that these living animals are likely to spread contagious disease if allowed to live. Where we order the slaughter of the animals, in the interest of the health of animals and of the people of the country at large-but only in such cases-we pay compensation. But in

this case, the discovery of the unfitness of the meat for human consumption is not made until the animal is dead and there is no further danger in the way of spreading disease; it. is simply the loss of the value of the carcass or of that part of the carcass which has to be destroyed. My hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie) spoke of the drovers of Ontario as having lost a very large sum of money. My own observation would lead me to believe that the figure the hon. member gives is much larger than could possibly have occurred. Those interested may talk that way, but no such figures as he mentions have been given to me, and I think that the figure is exaggerated. Of course, I do not mean that it is exaggerated by my hon. friend; I do not know from whom he got his information.
I have had the information from the chairman of the association.

They have not given me such large figures as that. I know they have made large payments and suffered great loss, but the incidence or the loss is not yet thoroughly established, and I think in some eases it is on the one hand, and in some cases on the other according to the bariruins that were made.
Mr. .1. A. CURRIE. I understand the courts have decided that the farmer is not responsible, because the distinction is made between selling a diseased animal and selling diseased meat. Then the question arises, whether the abattoir man or the butcher, or the drover is responsible. But the abattoir man endorses every cheque he issues that the animals are sold subject to inspection, and consequently the whole loss is thrown on the drover. To my mind, it is the consumer who benefits in the end, and. therefore, the beneficiary should pay for the protection. If the department approaches the matter from mat logical standpoint, it will reach a solution of the difficulty much quicker than by attempting to trace responsibilty from the time the bullock was born, in its passage through many owners, until it gets to the market.

I do not agree that the consumer is the principle one concerned, because it is the export trade of the country we are trying to protect. In the case of interprovincial trade it is the Canadian consumer, but this Act is chiefly intended to safeguard our large and important export trade which supports large industries in this country, which in their turn are of great value to the original producer, the farmer. Without this law the export trade would be in serious danger.
Mr. .1. A. CURRIE. I quite understand that but the man who is suffering at present Js the drover who is being driven out Mr. FISHER
of business. It is not in the interest of this country that the poor drover should be taxed $1,000 a year to protect the public from diseased meat. It is a hardship on them and if the minister considers the matter carefully and brings in legislation to remedy that hardship he will, I believe, meet with general support. The poor drover has a wife and family to support, his whole capital may be only $3,000, and if he has to pay $1,000 a year out of his business he s;mply will be driven to the wall. The minister should give this matter grave consideration and not take a stand one way or the other until he has thoroughly sifted all the facts. The government assumes the cost of protecting the lives of the people on the ocean, on the railways and in various other ways, and I do not see why they should not assume the cost of protecting the lives of the people in this case.

In considering this amendment without the original Act before vou, it is hard to thoroughly understand the intention of it. If any portion of the amendment is intended to deal with any portion of the subject that has been under discussion recently, I feel that if the hon. member for Simcoe is correctly stating the conditions in Toronto, he is certainly not stating them correctly with regard to Hamilton or many other places I know of. Nor is he stating the correct position of some drovers on the Toronto market. Our packers in the vicinity of Hamilton claim that they lose all the meat rejected by the insoectors, and while I have sympathy with any person who meets with a loss which might be averted, I cannot endorse the reasoning that the loss should be on the farmer. I think the drover who purchases the animal from the producer has the right to make all the examination and inspection he wishes before he buys the animal, but when he has bought the animal and taken possession of it the farmer's responsibility should cease. Then, when the drover sells on the market to the packer, unless he willingly agrees that he should stand the loss, I do not think the law should compel him. The packer on his part has the right to make the most minute inspection of the animal he wishes, and the moment he buys it and assumes possession the responsibility of the drover should cease. I am satisfied from the information I have had that the loss is now borne by the packer, and I think he is best able to stand it. I am quite satisfied that he gauges his buying and selling price by an estimate of that loss, and no doubt the producer and consumer pay in the end. I do not want the House to look upon the matter from the point of view that the-drover is standing that loss now. He may be in some eases where he agrees to, but
6*289

if it be a fact that be is bearing the loss then the law should be amended so that when a man buys and assumes possession of an animal the responsibility of the seller should cease.

I do not wish the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sealey) to run away with the idea that I am wishing to impose this loss upon any single section of the community. The hon. member says that the packer loses and. if that be so', I say it is a great hardship on the packer, and it is unjust. I am creditably informed the drovers have lost .$400,000, and that I say is a serious loss and a great injustice to them. We have been told, on the other hand, that the farmers have to pay the loss, and I quite agree that if that be so it is a great hardship on the farmer, because the farmer may have brought that animal as a young animal and it may have passed through two or three different hands, and it would be difficult to trace the first point from where the animal became diseased. It is a hardship then on the farmer. After the animal passes visual inspection the responsibility for the animal should pass to the owner. But when the matter is such a serious one and when it has such an important bearing upon the interests of the community, the community should hold itself responsible for a share of the loss. It is the community that is being protected, the safety and health of the people are being ensured, and I think the community should help in some degree to pay for the loss that is occasioned by reason' of their protection. I do not think the cost should be borne by either the farmer, the drover or the packer. It is neither fair, just nor equitable.
The transfer of the property after inspection should settle the responsibility.

I suppose there will be a variety of suggestions with respect to the inspection of beef. I have one or two complaints from my own county, one from a very prominent drover who complains that the drover is at a loss. For example, he goes to a farmer, buys a half dozen beef animals, gives his cheque for the animals, the cheque is taken to the bank, and the farmer receives his money. When the drover gathers his carload of cattle together, takes them to Toronto, and disposes of them to the abattoir, the abattoir people give him a cheque upon which is marked the condition that these animals are subject to government inspection, and if they fall below the government standard the abbatoir man goes back to the drover and asks for a recompense. The drovers in my section claim that they should be relieved in some way-I am not prepared to say how. The drovers venture to say that
the farmer should bear the loss if they can trace the animal back to the farmer. ' I do not agree with the drovers in that respect. It is a matter that should be very carefully considered. I have no doubt that it has been carefully considered by the minister, and I hope he will continue'to give it careful consideration. I believe that the government should take some considerable responsibility in this matter. I do not want to ask that the farmer should be the loser; I do not think he should be. I think it is a case where the farmer should not be the loser, I do not think the drover should be the loser, but it is a matter that should receive such consideration at the hands of the government as will result in the introduction of some amendment that will cause this loss to be shared by those who are entitled to pay it.

The question of the cheque paid to the drover, as described by the hon. gentleman, must be a matter of arrangement between the packer, and the drover. I do not think that parliament or the government should interfere with an arrangement of that kina. If the drover does not choose to take a cheque of that kind from the packer he need not do so.
I understand that the abbatoir people do not give any other cheques.
It may be a matter of coercion.

I speak subject to correction, but I understand that in Toronto, when a drover disposes of his cattle to the abbatoir people, the trade is based on the condition that the animals are subject to government inspection, and this condition is marked on every cheque.

Of course, the abbatoir people may be so strong, and have such a complete control over the trade that they can do that, but the drovers have a perfect right to say that they will not buy for an abbatoir that does that. It is a matter of private agreement. I know that in Toronto there is a system-I think it is managed by the Union Stock Yards Company-of insurance by which a small fee of twenty-five cents per head is paid in, and out of the fund thus secured losses are paid. I know that in England, where this question has been threshed out for years, a system of insurance has been arranged by which there is a small fee paid, and these losses are completely covered in that way. In Germany a similar system of insurance obtains, and all the parties engaged in the trade between the first sale of the animal to its final slaughter, and inspection, are insured in that way. I have not the full details of any of these schemes. I think that my director general of veterinary af-

fairs has the full details of the Toronto scheme, but I do not have them in my mind at the present moment. We have not the details of the English and German schemes. I think that is probably the best solution of the whole thing, but it would be extremely difficult for the government to interfere, and lay down rules or laws on a subject of this kind. My hon. friend must not think for a moment that I take either one side or the other. I am not taking sides against the drover or the packer. I appreciate the losses of all of them, and I would be extremely glad to see these losses equitably met. The way to do it seems to me to be on the insurance principle, or by a mutual arrangement between the parties who are engaged in the trade. I have not found my way to any proper, and effective interference in the matter on the part of the department. If I could find a way that seemed to be effective, and quite proper, and fair to all parties concerned I would be only too glad to consider it. But it is because I have not been able to find such a way that I have not proposed any legislation.

In connection with the cheques that are issued by the abattoirs, if these cheques are drawn, obliging the the drover to assume any loss that may afterwards occur. Now, while I am not a lawyer, I do not think they carry the obligation of the drover to make good these losses if any occur after delivery. But, if they do, as has been said by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) the drover should refuse to sell to the establishment which imposes such conditions. Perhaps those conditions are imposed by all of the packers. If they are it is a case of combination among the packers to impose an unfair condition upon the drovers and upon a section of the people that cannot very well help themselves under the circumstances. If that is a general condition, then it is a fit subject for inquiry, and prosecutions under the Combines Act, and it may call for the passage of legislation by this House to prevent such an unfair condition existing.

I am pleased to be present on this occasion when this interesting discussion is going on. There is no doubt that some one is suffering. I know that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is doing his best to find a solution. There is only one proper wray out of it, and that is for the government to pay the loss. You slaughter a man's cattle to protect his neighbour. Then, his neighbour should contribute to the loss. I think this is the only way to do it, although I realize the great difficulty there must be in carrying out such a plan. As we say in the cattle trade, it all depends on whose ox is being gored. But, there is no question Mr. FISHER.
that some one is losing. If the animal is destroyed entirely, some one loses on it, and I think the country should contribute in some way towards the loss whether the loser be the abattoir, the drover or the farmer. If the meat is destroyed for the benefit of the public, the public should contribute towards the recompense of the one who loses.

I agree with what the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) says. In my own county there was a case where a farmer had to destroy three or four of his cattle on account of some contagious disease. An inspector comes from Ottawa and says:	You have
to kill those animals, but it does not come within the category of those that are paid for.	.
'My hon. friend is in error. No officer of my department orders anybody to kill an animal unless we are prepared to pay the compensation given by law.
Supposing one of the officers of the department goes out and pronounces it a contagious disease, does the law not pirovide that the animal must be destroyed?
Not necessarily.
If it is a contagious disease, as I understand the law, the animal must be destroyed. Does not the man say that it must be destroyed? At all events in the interest of the public it must be destroyed.
No.

If the animal has a disease which makes it necessary to destroy it, the farmer must lose it. He comes to Ottawa and gets the officials to examine the animal, and the official requires the animal, in the interest of the community, to be destroyed.

Whenever we order an animal to be killed we pay compensation. We do not order the destruction of all animals which are effected with contagious diseases. Mange is a contagious disease, but we do not 'order a mangy animal to be killed. It is only when we order an animal to be killed that rve pay compensation.

This question of the health of the public seems to me to be a very big question, and this House ought to consider it very seriously. I am not very much interested in diseased cattle; in my county we do not have any; but I infer from what the minister said in the early part of this discussion, that the matter of regulating the sale of diseased meats rests very largely in the hands of the different

provinces. I do not pretend to be a constitutional lawyej-, but I would say that if it is possible the federal power ought to control the sale of all foods from one end of this Dominion to the other, as one province may be a little more zealous than another in protecting the public from diseased meats. There has recently been a great deal of discussion in the United States and Canada regarding cold storage systems, and this House, while it is discussing diseased meats, might very well at the same time consider that subject. We have learned from the press that the public have been eating meat, eggs, poultry and fish which have been in cold storage for two years. 1 myself have known fish which is I suppose the most delicate kind of food produced, and which has come from the Manitoba lakes, that has been stored in Chicago for three years and has then been sold to the public. This is a matter of very serious importance, and I think that Canada might well take the initiative in regulating in some way the cold storage system. I think there ought to be a law that would make it impossible for any one to hold meat or other food products in cold storage longer than a certain period. The date when any food product is put in cold storage should be tagged on it. I believe that the manner in which our cold storage systems have been allowed to store up meat and other food products has had a great deal to do with the increased cost of living. There has been some agitation on this subject in Montreal, and I understand that the provincial government have practically said that they cannot regulate the cold storage system, as it is a Dominion matter. If that is so, it is up to the Minister of Agriculture or the government to formulate a policy and introduce legislation to regulate these cold storage systems all over the Dominion and place them under strict government inspection.

The unsettled and chaotic state of the law in regard to the foods of the public, to which this discussion has led up, is just another voice crying out for the establishment of a bureau of public health. No man who has intelligently considered the question of protecting the life of our people, both adults and children, can fail to realize the deplorable loss of life all over Canada for the want of some guiding hand in protecting the people in the food they eat and the water they drink. As truly as the sun is shining, the day is coming, and it is not verv far distant, when a federal bureau of public health will be established. The public cry out for it, the government see the necessity for it, and I think there are only two individuals within a radius of a good many miles of the seat of government who are opposed to it. No man can look^at the meat exposed for sale in our meat markets
without seeing that much unfit food is sold. No man can see the conditions under which the milk supplied to our homes is produced and handled without concluding that there ought to be a reform there. I am not using extravagant language when I say that the awful slaughter of the innocents which goes on in Canada every summer during the hot weather, is crying aloud to this government to establish a bureau of public health. More Canadians die from the first to the fifth year than trom the fifth to the fifty-fifth; and the cause of this awful slaughter of children is in most cases impure food, impure milk, ignorance in feeding, ignorance in preparing food. I think the day ought not to be far distant when the government will undertake to educate mothers how to feed their babies and women generally how to cook our' food. There is no question on which we legislate that is of such importance as this question. You cannot make a nation without having healthy people, and you cannot have a healthy people unless you protect them in the food they eat in infancy and childhood. You have only to look at a baker's wagon going about the streets of this citv or anywhere else to get an idea of present conditions. I have watched a man carry into a house loaves of bread, with the same hands with which he has probably attended to his horse in the morning. and with a pair of mittens that have probably not been washed for months. I would not like to say how much of the filth - of the stable or the streets is in it but it is there. Look at the meat in the shops exoosed to every breeze that blows filth upon it; look at the candy that is sold to your children exposed in the same way. We should have an authority on public health that would regulate all these things. Those who know how to protect the public should protect the public who don't know. There are people who cannot be expected to be educated in these things and it is the duty of this government to protect them. To my mind this is a question of paramount importance. If we consider it only from a monetary point of view; if we consider the enormous loss every year from unnecessary sickness and death; if we had no higher motive than mere dollars and cents it is a profitable thing to preserve the lives of our people. Then from the humanitarian point of view consider its vast imnortance; consider the alleviation of distress, the prevention of sickness; consider the enormous number of babies that are dying in this country every year who should grow up to be men and women and gbod Canadians.

I do not think it is fair for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blackl to suggest that the Minister of Agriculture

should be placed in the humiliating, position of being forced to go round Canada to teach the women how to feed their babies.
I did not say that.

That is what I understood the hon. gentleman to say. I do not know whether the Minister of Agriculture has much experience in that line, but I judge from what I know of him-at least from what I have seen and heard of him that he has not yet sufficient experience to enable him to teach the women of Canada how to feed their babies on milk.
You show great appreciation.

Well, I do not like the minister to be placed in a false position. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Black) that a public health department should be established by the government because there is no doubt that a number of our people are developing tuberculosis and other diseases from eating diseased meats. In every constituency of the Dominion the old and diseased cattle are being sold for practically the value of the hide, and the meat is canned and sold. I feel very strongly that the Minister of Agriculture must change his attitude, and that he must, devise some scheme whereby the people of Canada will be protected in their food. He should not devote all his energy to the protection of the people in foreign countries who eat our exported meat. For some years the custom is that calves about a day old have been sold to these eanners, and the meat turned out as chicken. Does the minister know that that is going on at the present time?
Not in any place where our inspection goes on.
I tell the minister that they are being shipped every week right into Montreal, and his inspectors are inspecting them.
No.
I know men who have been shipping them there.
Does the hon. member state that calves of the character he describes are sent to Montreal, and are allowed to pass my inspectors. If he does I say it is not so.
Yes it is.
I deny that.
And they pass your in spection.
No.
I say they do.
Give me an instance.
I am not looking after your inspectors, and if you had proper inspectors it would not happen, but the trouble is that you appoint shoemakers.
I do nothing of the kind. There is no one acting as an inspector who is not a veterinary surgeon, except a few laymen
Ah.

Wait a minute-these men have been butchers, or something of that kind, and they are entirely under the control and management of the veterinary inspectors. I deny that any calves such as the *hon. member has described have been allowed to pass into Montreal by my inspectors.
The trouble is that you appoint a tailor, or a shoemaker, or somebody like that.
My hon. friend is again making a reckless statement.

I am not.
Mr. FISHER, Yes, you are.
You allow such men as Mr. Biclcerdike, the member for Montreal, St. Lawrence, to appoint that kind of men, instead of the proper men.
No, Mr. Bickerdike would not send me a man who is not of t*he right kind.
The member for 3t. Lawrence knows as well as I do if he would like to state it, that such calves as I have mentioned are going right into Montreal every week.

I must protest against that statement so far as Montreal is concerned. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) is entirely mistaken. That is not the class of food that is used in the city of Montreal. My good friend (Mr. Reid) made the statement that I have recommended men to the Minister of Agriculture who were not competent for their positions. Let me tell him that if I recommended a man to the Minister of Agriculture my recommendation would be sufficient for him not to get the job.
Hear, hear.

When many applicants for positions come to me for a recommendation I tell them they had better not have it because the minister would be sure to keep them out of the position. They get their recommendation from some Tory %nember on the other side of the

House. Let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) that the inspection in Montreal is first class in every way. The only objection I have to the thing is that when the government destroys a man's property in the interest of public health they do not pay him for it. As to Montrealers eating the class of food described by the hon. member (Mr. Reid) he is entirely wrong; most .of it is consumed in Ontario. It does not come to Montreal at at all.

I am greatly encouraged by the certificate given me by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, Montreal, (Mr. Bickerdike) that the Minister of Agriculture accepts recommendations to office from Tory members of parliament. While I cannot claim to have a very profound knowledge of this subject, I quite agree with my hon. friend that, in cases of this kind, where, as the result of an inspection made for the protection of the general public, a man who has bought in good faith- of course, I say nothing of those who have not acted in good faith-finds his merchandise confiscated, or condemned, and consequently confiscated, and thrown valueless on his hands, it would be perfectly fair and proper that, to some extent, at all events, he should receive compensation from the public so protected. If I understood the Minister of Agriculture, he stated a few moments ago, in answer to the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) that where it was found necessary to destroy a living animal for the protection of the public, compensation was invariably paid. Now, I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture what is the difference in principle between these two eases. In one case the living animal is destroyed for the protection of the public and compensation is paid; in the other case, the carcass of the dead animal is destroyed for the general protection-or rendered absolutely valueless-and no compensation is paid. It seems to me that, while this inspection is most desirable, the people who, for the protection of the public find their property destroyed, have a claim to reasonable compensation.

There is a very great difference between paying compensation when we order the living animal to be destroyed, and paying compensation when the dead meat is found to be unfit for food. In the case of the living animal, the owner may say that the animal can be cured, and the value not lost, but the veterinary authorities consider the risk to the public too great, and the slaughter of the animal is ordered. This not only prevents the spread of the disease, but is a step towards stamping out the disease altogether. In the case of hog cholera we have conquered the disease. In the case of glanders, we* have reduced it so much that the compensation paid now is only one-fifth of what it was when we began, and we hope within a year or two to get the disease completely within bounds. On the other hand, the dead animal cannot spread disease. The meat is a merchantable article which can be sold or not sold. It is in the interest of the public that it should not be sold, because, in many cases, the consumer could not know that it was diseased and unfit for food. Therefore, in the interest of the public, we order it to be condemned.	And
in regard to this Act this applies only to the export and interprovincial trade. The reason why we deal with interprovincial trade is because the provincial authorities in the province where the-animal is slaughtered could not control it in the province where it originated. The opinion that is given me by the Department of Justice, while no definite statement is made, is that it is probable that the question of public health and the control of food products in a particular locality, is rather under the control of the provincial authorities than of the Dominion. Therefore, we have avoided undertaking anything in connection with what I may call purely local affairs. We hold to the general principle that it is better the local authorities should deal with local matters; and for this parliament to undertake the-making of a general law, such as has been-suggested by my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) would be a new departure which, I must confess, I am not prepared to present to parliament, and would not like to see carried out. The question, of' course, is fraught with difficulty. When this law relating to meat packing was passed a few years ago, the question was thoroughly threshed out, and the House decided, without serious objection, on the-line which this law has taken. The amendments here proposed do not deal with the general principle, but are simply amendments of detail intended to facilitate the operation of the law.

I was not suggesting that the minister should extend the law so as to interfere with provincial affairs. And I am quite prepared to recognize that there are more reasons why it should be necessary to order the slaughter of the living animals than'can be cited for the condemnation of the dead carcass. But I fail to see that the minister has answered the question as regards the difference in principle. In both eases you are destroying a man's property for the protection of the public. While the consumer might be deceived in the meat he purchases if this inspection were not made, is it not equally true that the packer, when he buys diseased animals, is equally deceived? For. of course, we are speaking of cases in which the bad quality of the meat is ascertainable and ascertained only by pro-

fessional inspection after the animal is slaughtered. I am not saying a word for the man who, with his eyes open, buys animals that are diseased. But, when it comes to the government making an inspection of meat for the protection of the general public, and condemning-properly condemning-some meat as unfit for food, it seems to me that it would be quite proper that the public, for whose protection this is done, should compensate the individual who, acting in perfect good faith, is made to suffer that the public may be protected.

Possibly we have drifted away from the subject which was brought to our attention earlier in the day by the Minister of Agriculture. At the same time, I feel sure that the time has not been wasted, for information has been given to members of this committee, and I hope it will find its way to the country. The minister was good enough to explain the^ system of compensation under the Contagious Diseases Act where animals become infected, and have to be destroyed. I have just one complaint to make with regard to the law 'as it is now framed, namely, that not only should the animal that is ordered to be destroyed by the government official be paid for, but that other animals in the same herd that may have died before the government inspector has reached the farm, should also be paid for. Now I am going to _ cite a case with which the minister's chief veterinary is quite familiar. Remember I am not taking exception to the administration of the law, but to the law itself. On the 11th day of the month a farmer noticed that his hogs were sick, and he called in the nearest veterinary who, by the way, is the quasi official of the government, because subsection 2 of section 3 of the Act respecting infectious or contagious diseases of animals, says:
Any veterinary surgeon practising in Canada should immediately, on ascertaining that an animal is labouring under an infectious or contagious disease give similar notice-
To the notice he gives to the minister, -to the nearest veterinary inspector.
So I say the veterinary is a quasi official of the government, and the government should in some way be responsible for any neglect of duty on his part. In the case I refer to, the farmer called in the veterinary on the 11th day of the month. He examined a carcass, and I understand a portion of it was sent to Ottawa for inspection. Before the officer of the government reached the farmer to examine his hogs, some ten days had elapsed, I think the veterinary from Ottawa did not reach there until the 21st day of the month. In the meantime, out of a herd of twenty-one hogs fifteen or sixteen had died, and only five or

six hogs remained which were ordered to be slaughtered. I understand the government paid, or promised to pay, and will, I presume, pay for those animals that were slaughtered. But what about the other two-thirds of that man's hogs which died before the veterinaary reached the place, and for which the farmer gets no compensation, though he had done his duty in the matter. My contention is that so long as compensation is to be granted, and so long as people carefully observe the law, and give notice to the proper officials, a man whose animals die before the inspector reaches there, and before the slaughter is ordered by the government inspector, should receive compensation for those that died previous to the inspector's arrival. I think the minister would not go far astray if he amended the law so as to permit of compensation being granted under conditions of this kind. The minister may tell me that he would be flooded with applications. Suppose he is. The object of the law is to stamp out disease, and I think the country can better afford to pay compensation for all these animals rather than that a poor tenant farmer should be compelled to sustain the loss himself. Not only does he sustain the loss, but he is actually prohibited for the next three months from keeping an animal of the same kind upon his farm, and probably loses the use of that class of product for the whole twelve months.

This subject of course is entirely aside of the question before the committee, but I am not complaining of that. I may remind the hon. gentleman that when the law was amended so as to permit payment for animals killed by order of the department, perhaps not the hon. gentleman himself, but others around him, pointed out that unless that provision was carefully safeguarded it might lead to great abuse, and I promised that no compensation would be paid for animals slaughtered except they were slaughtered by order of one of my permanent officers. In the case my hon. friend refers to, the veterinary was not an official of the department in any sense of the word. My hon. friend says he is a paid official. We have given him authority to issue certain certificates, but that is all, he is not an official authorized to order the slaughter of animals. The law says that every veterinary who hears of a contagious disease must report it to us. but that does not constitute him a government official in any way. I can understand my hon. friend's dissatisfaction, when one of his constituents perhaps has suffered in the way he has described, and there may be occasions where it would be only fair and just to pay some compensation. But I fear that any relaxation in the law in that respect would lead to such demands, and

such difficulty in the verification of the reasons for slaughtering an animal, that enormous expense would be incurred which .would be unjust to the community at large who would have to pay the expense.

Although the question of compensation may not arise under this Bill, I may perhaps be allowed to sav that I agree with the sentiments which have been expressed by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), to the effect that the present law is quite inadequate. Many cases have arisen, and do arise, where, through the action of the government or its officials, serious direct loss is suffered by farmers and no compensation is paid, and where, I am sorry to say, I do not think any effort is being made in the direction of paying compensation. I have rather a pointed case in my own county which I drew to the attention of the House last session, and have brought it to the attention of the department before, a case in which compensation has been refused. I think if there ever was a fair, just and reasonable case, to use the minister's language, in which compensation should be paid, the case I have submitted, and will again mention, is that case. In November, 1908, either one or two carloads of cattle were ordered for export from Fergus to Liverpool, fine cattle, all ready for export. At Niagara Falls, on the frontier, a veterinary inspector of this government stopped them, examined the car and reported, not that an animal was diseased, but that he suspected that one of the animals had the mange. The shipment was delayed at the Falls. It was ordered from there back to Toronto, for some reason that I have not yet been able to ascertain, from Toronto ordered back to Fergus, there it was kept for a considerable length of time, three or four weeks, the farmer had to procure special stables and to comply with the special quarantine regulations, and in the end it turned out that the animal was not diseased and did not have mange. The whole loss arose from the mistake of the inspector of the government at Niagara Falls. The farmer lost his opportunity of making a sale, he lost his freight from Fergus to Niagara Falls and back via Toronto, he was put to large expense for providing special stables and complying with the quarantine regulations; in fact, his loss has run from $1,000 to $1,200. That is directly attributable to the action of the inspector who made the mistake. Why should not the government compensate in a ' case of that kind? A man might make a mistake and act bona fide and I have no doubt that it was a bona fide mistake. Why should the farmer bear tlie loss? The minister informs me that it was for the security of the public. Well, then, why should the public not pay? If the animals
had been slaughtered two thirds of the value would have been paid, but as the matter stands to-day the man has lost from $1,000 to $1,200 on one shipment through no fault of his own, he has a fair, just and reasonable case and I think that either by special vote or otherwise that claim should be paid.
All I have to say in regard to that particular case is that it was not a case of slaughter at all under Animals Compensation Act, and we have not the right to pay compensation for that loss.
You should have the right.

The discussion has taken a very wide Tange and has introduced a good many questions that are of a very complex nature. I just wish to make a few remarks in regard to compensation. The government, I am sure, deserve credit for appointing inspectors to inspect meats and animals which are slaughtered in our slaughter-houses, and I presume that when thev appointed these inspectors_ they had little idea of the number of animals that

would be found to be diseased and the loss that would fall upon our packing-houses. As to whether the packing-houses or the farmers should be remunerated is certainly a very difficult question to determine. Primarily, I suppose, the farmer is liable but after the stock leaves the farm it is not always easy to trace the particular farm to which the loss is attributable and the fact at once is presented to our mind that the farmer cannot be made responsible. The drover certainly should not be, and those who conduct the packing-houses, 1 think, are unfairly dealt with when they are compelled to stand all the loss.
Do the packing houses stand the loss?

Yes, they do in most cases. I have in my mind especially the packing houses that kill hogs. I know' as a matter of fact that they have sustained the losses up to the present time in almost every instance, if not altogether. If the government were to undertake to meet these losses it would be ratheT difficult to determine what should be the proper amount of compensation. The packing house men might make a demand for compensation that would perhaps be more than would be fair. Some portions only of hog carcases are condemned, and the loss is sometimes comparatively small on individual animals. But w'hen the staff of inspectors is ample in the various packing houses they could arrive probably at a fair basis of valuation, and I think that the government might fairly undertake to compensate the packing houses, say, to the extent of 50 or 75 per cent of the loss without incurring the danger of paying them more than should be paid. I think that the consensus of this House and the opinion of the country generally would be such as to justify the government in taking the matter up, and, in a measure, compensating those who are compelled to lose on account of the diseases which are to be found to exist amongst animals. Of course, I know there is a great work to be done in the education of farmers in regard to the better ventilation of stables and the better caring for their stock in order to prevent the loss which is occurring from diseased animals, and unless the farmers are made to bear some of the loss perhaps the incentive will not be as strong as it should be to compel them to adopt the best possible methods of caring for their stock. If the packing houses feel that they are only being remunerated to the extent of, say, 50 or 75 per cent, they must pay that much less for the stock which they purchase from the farmers, and the farmers must expect to obtain less for their stock than if it is known that the stock is free, or compara-tivelv free, of disease. The packing houses,

after a year or two years' investigation and inspection, can determine fairly correctly what the percentage of loss is. But I think the best solution of this question w'ould be to pay the abattoirs a fair percentage, and the drovers who purchase from the farmers should enlighten the farmers, and the farmers should be led to understand that if their animals are absolutely free from diseases they would obtain even a better price than they are obtaining under the present regulations. I know' the government has done and is doing valuable and important work in educating the farmers in the care of milk, and the result is that the conditions under which the milk of this country is now' handled are infinitely better than they w'ere some years ago. It is the rule rather than the exception, that in every dairying district in Ontario the stables are thoroughly up to date in every respect, the ventilation perfect, and the dairy properly equipped w'ith every modern appliance. Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe this to be a very important discussion because it deals with the protection of every class of the community. It is a question of very great financial concern also, and anything that can be done by the government to properly distribute the loss as well as to better educate the people must prove most valuable in connection with this branch of our agricultural industry.

I direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the particular case cited by the hon. member for Wellington as being worthy of further consideration. In that case the farmer lost $1,200 through the neglect or inability of officials appointed by the minister and in such a case it appears to me only fair that the government should compensate the farmer for that loss. An item of $1,200 is a very important consideration to a farmer. I can speak with a good_ deal of sympathy as to that ease because''I know' a farmer who through the neglect of the government officials lost to the extent of about $1,500. The officials were advised of the case, but it took them four days to get there, and w'hen they arrived they ordered the animals destroyed, but about 20 per cent of the animals had died during the four days' delay. I believe that if that farmer took an action in the courts he would recover damages because of the neglect of the officials of the department.

On the question of amending the Act in the direction of stamping all food that goes into cold storage, any one wdio has paid attention to w'hat has appeared in the press during the last few' months must conclude that great injury is being done to the trade of the country by the abuse of this cold storage system which amounts practically to a

conspiracy to enhance prices. Then, there is the health aspect of the case, because in my judgment as a medical man, food may be so deteriorated that it becomes unhealthy if it is kept in cold storage for an undue length of time. We had a statement as to the length of time food products arc kept in cold storage in Chicago and Kansas, but I saw a statement recently that the carcases of animals were kept for two years in cold storage in Montreal. It is very easy to verify that statement and it should he inquired into. It seems to me that it is the imperative duty of the Department of Agriculture to amend the law so as to compel the stamping of the date upon all food that is put into cold storage, and, providing that it shall not be kept there longer than a certain period. This is an opportune time now to legislate in that direction.
At- one o'clock committee took recess.
Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

A matter was brought to my attention some time ago which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. A farmer sold a very valuable beef animal to a drover. Some ten days or two weeks afterwards, the drover, who had taken his cargo to Montreal, sent a notice to the farmer that one of the animals he had bought from him had tuberculosis, and asked the farmer to refund the purchase money. The farmer had no evidence other than the word of the drover that it was his animal that was diseased, but rather than go into a lawsuit he decided to refund the money, amounting to some $80. He asked me if I would bring the matter up here at an opportune time, and find out if some remedy could not be provided for cases of this' kind. He hacl raised a great many beef cattle, and so far as he could see all the animals he sold to the drover were in perfect health. The animal in question may have been his or it may have been somebody else's. I want to bring the matter to the minister's attention, and ask him if he thinks the farmer should suffer the loss of his animal under these circumstances?
Not knowing all the circumstances, I could not say anything about it. I suppose it is a matter for the courts to decide.

It seems to me that a farmer in selling his animals to drovers runs a great deal of risk. When the drover tells him that any of his animals are diseased, he has to lose the money or else perhaps go into court, and if he handles thoroughbred cattle he probably prefers to pay the money than go into court. I should imagine that a drover should be compelled
to give some evidence that an animal is diseased, or else notify the farmer immediately after the purchase.
r
I should think that if the farmer defended himself, the drover would have to produce some evidence before he could collect; but I would not care to give a legal opinion on the matter.

What is right and honourable, and just should be law. Now, the government appoint Inspectors to inspect meat. They do that for the benefit of the general public. The government, representing the general public, pay these inspectors, and it is through them that the general public receive the benefit. Those who receive the benefit should pay the cost. The government, in appointing inspectors, have gone a certain distance. Any one who employs another person to do work for him, whether the government or an individual, is responsible for what that servant may do under their instructions. When an animal is condemned, there may be considerable difficulty in knowing to whom it belonged in the first place. It is utterly im-IKissible that one hog among 400 or 500 can be traced to the farmer from whom it was purchased. Even if that could be done, a farmer who had any suspicion that the animal was diseased, would not offer it for sale to a drover who would be likely to take it to a point where it would be inspected. The result is that diseased animals are retained on the farm. In that way the present practice really results in propagating disease, because the animal thus retained by the farmer is sold to the local butcher, and by the local butcher to the people of the neighbourhood. Thus meat for export is being inspected while the meat being sold to our Canadian citizens is not being inspected.
Whose fault is that?

I am just pointing out what the natural result of the present condition of affairs is. I am not saying that it is anybody's fault in particular. The meat supplied to our Canadian citizens is not inspected. They get the discarded beef, while the inspected meat is exported. The consequence is that if the farmer is made responsible, the result which I have pointed out will naturally occur, while if the government would pay a percentage of the value of the meat that is condemned, when it gets into the hands of the final purchaser, the farmer would not have 'such a fear to sell his animals, and more effective inspection would take place. I think that the government, as representing the general public, which is being benefited, should pay a percentage, say 50 or 75 per cent, of the value of the animal destroyed. The farmer would not be subject

to the loss, the drover, wlio now receives cheques which are only payable on certain conditions, would also be relieved, and the man who packs or cans the meat would not be such a heavy loser as he is. I quite approve of the government appointing these inspectors; I am one of those who think that the government cannot do too much along that line. I believe that a bureau of health should be established, and should 'be put under the charge of a man who would take a position in this country at some future time equal to that of Koch or Pasteur in Eurpoe. I believe we have in Canada young men of enthusiasm who are competent for such a position. Then we would not have so many halting attempts, and failures as we have at the present time. Such a man would make his work his life study, and the result would be that a great deal of good would he done, and a great many valuable lives saved.

My hon. friend says that the local market has all the diseased meat thrown upon it. If it has, that is due to the laxity of provincial or municipal inspection. The municipal authorities have JuM as much power to inspect as the Dominion Agricultural Department, and if taey do not do it, it is their own fault, and I must protest against responsibility being thrown on the Dominion parliament or the Dominion government for a duty which is the duty of the provincial authorities. If that is to be thrown upon us we ought to assume the whole range of provincial legislation and administration. I must protest against the idea that because the provincial government do not do their duty therefore this government should do that duty. If it is their duty, and they neglect it then it becomes the duty of the provincial electors, and supporters of whatever government it may be, Liberal or Conservative, to force that provincial government to do its duty, and not to appeal to the administration of this government to perform a duty which is essentially provincial or municipal. It is our duty to deal with the export trade, and we are trying to do it, and do it effectually, and I believe to-day that the complaints which are being made are largely due to the fact that the local inspection is not as severe as our inspection. Severity of inspection is quite in line with what my hon. friend has said, and I take it he is supporting me in making a severe, and properly efficient inspection. If the local authorities are not doing the same thing, that is no reason why I should be asked to do their duty, and their work.

I certainly am supporting the minister in having a very rigid inspection, but I am not supporting him in the idea of destroying property for Mr. T. CHISHOLM
the general benefit of the people of Canada and not making compensation, because the result is that the effect of the loss goes back through the different purchasers until finally it reaches the farmers, and there as a consequence the diseased meat i3 allowed to stagnate, as it were. I have no doubt the provincial authorities may possibly be responsible, but the result is that the effort that is being made by the minister in these lines is increasing the trouble that we have from the inefficiency of the local authorities if there is such inefficiency. The present system is undoubtedly increasing that trouble. There is no doubt that by throwing the responsibility on the producer, on the farmer finally, the local market is congested with the diseased meat, and a medical man who understands what he is talking about, must understand that it is a very serious thing to the people of Canada. We can better afford to pay a percentage of the cost of this diseased meat when it is found at its final resting place where the animals are slaughtered much better than to have our people living on it and being injured. Those who are benefited should pay. The general public are benefited, and, therefore, the general public should pay the cost. I will not say that they should pay the whole cost, because that might lead to irregularities, Jnit we should certainly pay a percentage of the cost, and it should be paid to those who slaughter the animals. We know it is almost impossible when a steer or fat beast is leaving the farm to know what diseases it may have. When the animal comes io be slaughtered, the defects will be disclosed, and I quite approve of what the minister is doing. His course, however, is having results that he evidently did not intend. I think the chief source of difficulty lies in not paying a percentage on the discarded meat.

I think we are dealing with matters under Dominion Acts that have a local effect. For instance, we have our inspection of canned fruits and canned goods of all kinds. That is an article that enters into local consumption, and yet it is inspected under this government.
When it is for export.
You go into a man's grocery and test his goods as to purity, &c., you deal with them as inspectors
Not under this Act.

No, not under your department. It seems to me you will never rid the country of diseased cattle until there is some more definite understanding as to what remuneration will be given by the government for animals destroyed. I can quite understand the necessity of guarding against the possibility of extrava-

gant values, &c., that would be imposed on the government if they opened the gate to any considerable extent. The value of animals would increase very rapidly if they were being paid for by the government. A case came to my notice a few days ago on which I would like to have some information. A farmer having a large herd of cattle called a sale and sold to bidders in different parts of the country. It turned out that the cattle were badly diseased with tuberculosis, they went into different neighbourhoods miles apart, into different herds. I know one man who found that the animals were diseased shortly after he purchased them. He called in an inspector, the animals were condemned and killed for tuberculosis. What recourse has that man against the man who sold the animals?
I would not give a legal opinion.	.

I will have to pay for my law. There is more of this disease in some localities than we are aware of, and I do not think we will get rid of it until we give the people more of an incentive to make it known that their animals have the disease. A farmer battling hard to make a living realizes that if it is known that he has tuberculosis among his cattle, his herd will be destroyed and he will be put out of business. As long as that condition exists, he will not be inclined to make known the fact that his animals are diseased, but if it was possible to arrange it so that the country would not be imposed on, it would be a good thing to grant compensation. If it cost the country two or three millions to get rid of the disease, it would be a wise expenditure.
I do not think that compensation for dead animals would help to get rid of the disease.
It would have some effect. I am aware that ventilation of stables, &e., all enter into this matter, but it seems to me that the other would be a more effective way.
Make the farmer raise good cattle.

You cannot make him do that any more than you can make him have good children. It is all very well for men to talk about things as they ought to be, but public men have to deal with things as they are.
How many inspectors has the minister in Toronto?
Inspectors and assistants iu Toronto, about 22 or 23.
Has the Minister in his department any information as to how the abattoir people pay the cattle dealer for his cattle?
We have no records in the department.

Does not my hon. friend think that it would be a fair subject for investigation? There might be a tendency toward a monopoly. I have a letter from a constituent in which he states that the abattoir people in the city of Toronto always give a cheque in payment of cattle to the cattle dealer, with the reservation that these cattle must pass inspection, but that the cattle dealer does not give any such cheque to the farmer.

I do not think a case of that kind is a matter for interference on the part of the department. I do not see how we could dictate to people making a bargain or trade arrangement as to what they should do. If there is a combine, then that would be a subject for investigation under the Combines Act. But I do not think it is the function of the Department of Agriculture to investigate a bargain which exists between a cattle drover and the abattoir company.

I agree with the minister that it would not be the duty of the government, if they found such a state of things, to take any steps to correct it. But I do say that the government could afford valuable information in discussing a question of this kind. If there is such an understanding with the abattoir people, then it removes the loss and responsibility from the abattoir people and places it either upon the farmer or upon the cattle dealer.

I realize that it is a difficult matter to adjust the loss and responsibility between the farmer and the drover. I do not mean to. say that a farmer who sells a diseased animal should not lose that animal, he certainly should. But many farmers, such as the one I referred to a moment ago, put animals on the market perfectly satisfied that they are in a healthy condition. I am satisfied that this man I referred to, if he had the least suspicion that an animal was diseased, would never have offered it for sale, because he is a very large breeder, and has some of the best cattle in the province, and it would never pay him to put a diseased animal on the market. Yet the drover goes out into the country and buys 50 or 100 head of cattle and ships them to Montreal, and if he finds when he gets there that some of his animals are diseased, it is unfair to require him to suffer the entire loss. He cannot bring them back to the farmers, because he does not know which farmer sold the cattle. If the government orders those animals to be destroyed, I think they should make compensation in some way.

This Inspection Act has been on the statute-book for two or three years, and I beard the Minister of Agriculture say, in answer to my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) that he had twenty-one

inspectors in the city of Toronto. I would like to know how many inspectors he has in the city of Halifax.
I do not think we have any there. There are no establishments in Halifax which have asked for an inspection.

It is rather an odd thing that, in the city of Halifax, which is quite an exporting town, sending goods abroad from the province of Nova Scotia and also from Prince Edward Island which are sent to Halifax, that this Act has been on the statute-book for two or three years, and we have never had it enforced. We never had any intimation of an enforcement until about two months ago, when the collector of customs at Halifax got instructions not to permit any goods to be exported to any foreign country unless they had the government inspector's stamp on them. This is rather an odd thing to do, after the Act has been on the statute-book for two or three years.
