It seems to me it would have been up to the government to make some provision for carrying out that Act and to give the people reasonable notice of their intention, so that they might have their goods and canned meats ready for inspection and ready for export. Now we get an intimation from the collector of customs that no goods can be exported from the city of Halifax unless they have the government inspector's stamp, and the consequence is that our export trade is closed up. There is nothing to prevent them selling their goods to the people of Nova Scotia or of any other province; the government apparently does not care whether our native Canadians are killed off or not. But the very instant you start to sell to the West Indies or any other foreign country, that .instant the government becomes anxious for the welfare of the foreigners, and proceeds to provide inspected food for them. Some application was made to the department, and a letter was written to the Minister of Agriculture to which he replied, and in his reply he was good enough to say that the junior member for Halifax did not know what he was talking about, and did not know what he ivas writing about, or he would have known that there was an Act on the statute-book for two or three years that demanded this inspection. Well, all I have to say is that if the government have put that Act on the statute-book and allowed it to be broken for two or three years, I would not like to tell what I think of their action, because the chairman might say I was out of order. But I think it is only fair to ask that those who have been sending goods to foreign markets for two years, should now be allowed at least two or" three months in which to dispose of their present season's goods of cured meats and canned goods on hand, and be allowed to ship them

to the markets they have hitherto been supplying without any complaint; and then let these provisions be made applicable to Nova Scotia. The collector of customs at Halifax is an excellent officer who has had much experience in the export trade, and I think the government might well have allowed him to exercise some discretion in this matter. I hopb that the Minister of Agriculture will see his way, by some method that is reasonable and fair, to permit the export of these goods to go on for a month or two longer. I ask that especially in view of the fact that no complaint has ever been received from the foreign market of the goods supplied.
Another thing is that, as I understand, we have no inspector there. A gentleman in Halifax told me-I will not mention 'his name, as it is not necessary, and no doubt the Minister of Agriculture or some of his officers will know to whom I refer-that he wrote to the department to have an inspector appointed to inspect the abattoir in which he was killing animals, particularly lambs, and sheep, commencing with the month of May. He was told that he could have an inspector if he made an application; but, on making an application, he was told that he would have to give some guarantee of the quantity he would be prepared to export. I have not the correspondence here, but it could be got within a day or two. While this gentleman kills many cattle and sheep and is to some extent an exporter, a great deal of his product is sold to people in Halifax who are exporters. He frequently -sends to other provinces also. I understand that meat of this class cannot be sold in the province of Ontario unless it has been inspected. I am not complaining of the inspection; the only complaint I make is that the people had not sufficient notice of the intention to enforce the Act. I think that, in all fairness, some opportunity should be afforded to our people to get rid of the goods they prepared at a time when it was not generally known that the law would be carried into effect. The collector of customs of Halifax is a man who has the confidence of the people, and 1 am sure he ha3 t<he confidence of the government, and I would suggest that the matter be left in his hands in the meantime. It will be a great advantage to the city of Halifax, and to the province of Nova Scotia, and also, I believe, to the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick as well.

I do not wonder that the hon. member (Mr. Crosby) should be anxious about the matter to which he has referred. This Act is new to him, but no complaint can be made of him on that gcore. The facts he has mentioned, whilo

in the main correct, are astray in some important points. In the first place, the Customs Department was notified of the coming into force of thi3 Act, and the Customs Department, I believe, notified all its collectors. But the customs collector at Halifax does not appear to have taken any account of it, at any rate, no report of export was made to us until recently. We were obliged to draw the attention of the customs collector to the provisions of this Act, and intimate that the law must be enforced. This Act deals with exports, and interprovincial trade only. The people of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick do as they like about selling animals, or meats within these provinces; that is a matter of provincial legislation and administration;-the subject has been discussed here to-day, though, I believe, my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) was not present. To facilitate the work under the Act in the maritime provinces, and acting under power given by the law the maritime provinces were regarded as one province for the purposes of this meat inspection law. Consequently, sending from one of the maritime provinces to another would not be considered interprovincial trade under this Act. This was done at the request of the people there. A little while ago- I have forgotten the exact date-a certain firm in Halifax received some goods from Prince Edward Island which they wished to export to the West Indies. The customs collector said they could pot export these goods without a certificate of inspection. These goods had not been inspected for the purpose of sending them from Prince Edward Island to Halifax. We are quite ready to inspect goods and to appoint an inspector in Halifax, or anywhere else where there are goods for export business. But the goods referred to in this case were not in condition for our officers to inspect them. We cannot inspect goods which are turned into bacon or packed in cans; inspection must take place not merely of the whole carcass together, but of the carcass with what are called the attachments, the heart, liver, lungs,. &c. These goods were in Halifax ready for export and it was impossible for us to inspect them a3 required under the law. Whenever animals are being (Slaughtered for export, it is our duty to provide" an inspector, and we >have never failed to do so. The hon. member (Mr. Crosby) mentions the case of one gentleman in Halifax who asked for an inspector. We asked him whether his goods were for export or not. We have had a number of requests from local butchers to send inspectors, but it is not our duty to inspect for the local market. We asked that gentleman whether he was going to be exporting regularly, so that we would be 201
justified in appointing an inspector for the purpose of inspecting his goods for export. We have not yet received that information. We did not ask for a guarantee. We did not ask for any statement of just how much he was exporting, although we had to ask to find out what his trade was expected to be. That was necessary before we could appoint an inspector because for all we knew the trade might be a local trade and we could not appoint an inspector to deal with that. That is the reason we delayed sending an inspector. When we get that information from that gentleman, and if he shows us that he is engaged legitimately in the export trade, we will provide an inspector at once. That explanation perhaps has given my hon. friend the information regarding the details of this matter, which, of course, 'speaking from memory, he could not be expected to have, but I can assure him that we are just as anxious to provide all facilities for inspecting in Halifax or anywhere else in the maritime provinces as we are in Ontario. If, to-day, there is no inspection in Halifax it is simply because we were not aware of the existence of packing houses or establishments packing for the export trade. We are ready to give an inspector and to inspect immediately they are doing that trade. But, it is impossible, after the [DOT] animals have been slaughtered and the meat cut up and packed for us then to inspect it efficiently and be able to judge whether it is diseased or not. That is the reason why we could not give a certificate, for these goods for the purpose of export. That the collector of customs, estimable and competent for his work though he may be, would be' able to examine these goods and give a certificate for export is quite out of the question. Thisj can only be done by a properly qualified veterinary surgeon and the Act requires that the certificate shall only he signed by a properly qualified veterinary surgeon. Even though I thought it advisable the statute would forbid me to do it.

I may not know very much about this Act and I am very glad to have the information which the Minister of Agriculture has given me in regard to it, but I do know something about business. I must say that an Act which has been on the statute-book for upwards of two years and never put in force until within perhaps the last six or eight weeks would seem to me not to be an Act based on very good business principles. I would not consider it good business were I dealing with the affairs of the country, and I would say to the Minister of Agriculture, although he is always busy when he is being addressed by some one from the eastern part of Canada

I must protest; that is not a fair insinuation. I pay just as much attention to the people from the eastern part of Canada as I do to people from any other part, and if for the moment I was asking a question of my officer it was not because I was not listening to the hon. gentleman.
When I was addressing the committee a few minutjs ago I noticed that the Minister of Agriculture and a gentleman near him were talking all the time.
Because l was asking questions in regard to what the hon. gentle-was saying to inform myself so that I might answer him.

After the reference that the minister made to me, to the effect that what I said was of very little account, I would think that it would not be worth while to ask any questions of anybody in order to answer me. I confess* I do not know much about the matter but I do know something about business. This Act does not strike me as being a very good one any way. An Act, which, while providing particularly for the inspection of all kinds of goods going out of Canada, makes no provision for the inspection of the goods at the time they should be exported, seems a very extraordinary Act. An Act that is on the statute-book for upwards of two years and is never put in force until the last three or four weeks does not seem to me to be an Act to which the government attach very much importance; otherwise, they would have put it ini force long before this. That Act having been on the statute-book some three years and not having been put in force, surely the foreign customers of the Dominion would not have suffered very much by that same condition prevailing until the people interested had shipped the goods which they had prepared for export. There are two large concerns in Halifax putting up goods particularly for certain markets abroad. Their brand is asked for and their goods are accepted on the strength of this brand, sold in the markets in competition with goods from every part of the world, and I may add that they compare favourably with goods produced elsewhere. The people of the West India markets to which these goods are principally sent know the goods and they, are willing to come to Halifax and buy them. But we cannot sell these goods because they have not government inspection and there is no way of getting government inspection. I quite understand that if you are to have an inspection of swine or cattle the animals must be inspected before they aTe killed. But there should be some way whereby the people putting up these preserved meats, hams, bacon, &c., should be Mr. CROSBY.
permitted to ship these goods. When I referred to the collector of customs I did not suggest that he should be allowed to inspect the goods; it was a question of the collector of customs being able to distinguish between a creditable packer, a man who had a reputation of putting up high-class goods, and a stranger who might come in there and about whose goods he did not know anything. The collector of customs might be able to say of the goods, of a well known packer:	I know these
goods, they have always met with commendation, they have been always well received in the foreign market and sold there on equal terms with goods from any other part of the world and therefore thev might be allowed to be exported out of Canada without fear of any difficulty or trouble arising. That was my reason for referring to the collector of customs. The Minister of Agriculture states that the Act has been on the statute-book and that the collector at Halifax did no*t put it in force. All I have to say in regard to that is that the customs house at Halifax is a very important custom house and the collector is a very important man, perhaps second to none in the Dominion. I am quite sure that if he had been notified by the Department of Customs or the Department of Agriculture he would have carried out the instructions of the department, but not having been notified he did not know anything about this Act until about three or four weeks ago and therefore the Act has, only recently been put into force. The Act, having been on the statute-book for two or three years and it not having been put in operation, surely this condition can be continued for a month or six weeks to give the mercantile community of Halifax, Nova Scotia and perhaps New Brunswick an opportunity of getting rid of the goods which they have put up for certain markets. These markets want them, their customers want them and are ready to take delivery in the city of Halifax and it* is unfair that the government should prevent trade and commerce in this way.

I would bring to the attention of the minister what is at least one inequality in the working out of this Act. It seems to me that the person who is really hurt by the operation of the Act has not yet been heard, because the man who loses the money as a result of the inspection of meat, is the packer, and I think I can safely say he is the only one who loses. Inspection takes place only with regard to meat for export, and it takes place in the abattoir, where the packing is done. The number of packers in Canada is comparatively few, but they have reasonably large establishments, and it is quite impossible for them to tell from whom they buy any particular lot of hogs

or cattle. They certainly cannot identify from whom they purchase the hogs and generally speaking it is not reasonably possible to identify from whom the cattle are purchased. As these animals go through the various stages of slaughtering and packing the inspector stands there and condemns a whole carcass as tubercular, or he may only condemn parts of that carcass, and the meat so condemned is rejected, and its value lost to the packer. The packer has no guarantee or warrant, and he cannot look to the drover from whom he bought, so that he alone is the loser. I quite approve of a proper inspection of meat for export, so that our exports may be all of first-class quality, and in so much as that commodity is an advertisement for the trade of this country generally, it is not just that the packer should be the man who has to lose everything. It seems to me that the system of government compensation for slaughtered animals should in some way be extended so as to compensate the packer. His establishment is a clearing house for diseased animals, and as it is in his possession the meat is found when it is condemned, he is the loser. I am not altogether of the minister's opinion that this is not a matter for Dominion interference. Under section 95 of the British North America Act, the Dominion has concurrent jurisdiction with the provinces in all matters regarding agriculture, and, if the minister takes control to regulate the export trade under the authority of the trade and commerce provision of that Act, I do not see how he gets away from the responsibility of protecting the public against diseased animals, under the clause which gives the Dominion control over agriculture. Then again, if it be a misdemeanour to have diseased animals for sale in one's possession, it would come under the Criminal Code, which would give the Dominion jurisdiction. I hardly think the Dominion government can clear its skirts by saying that it has no authority to inspect meat for domestic consumption. Look at the conditions: a man is engaged in the business of slaughtering hogs, which he sends to all places within a certain province, and he is not subject to inspection, but his next door neighbour, who packs for export or interprovincial trade, must submit to a rigid inspection. The inequality is so glaring that I do think the government should take the matter into consideration, and, if possible, equalize the present conditions. The farmer is not hurt, because any diseased animals he disposes of he gets paid for.
What about those he cannot dispose of?

He would have to bear the loss, I suppose, in such a ease.
But, even where the government orders his animals to be destroyed, the farmer gets some substantial compensation.
[DOT] They do not get compensation in some cases.
But that is the law.
They get compensation if the slaughter of the animal is ordered by one of our inspectors.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonell) is mistaken as to compensation being paid for hogs. If the hogs are alive and they are condemned to be destroyed, the farmer gets compensation, but he does not get any compensation if the dead hog is rejected by the government inspector. In that case he has to stand the loss just the same as the packer.
It is only in cases of packing for export that inspection takes place, and therefore it can only be in such case that rejection takes place.
The farmer gets some compensation when live hogs are condemned, but he gets no compensation when dressed hogs are condemned.
The farmer may kill his hogs and send them dressed to the market, and if it is found that these dressed hogs were diseased the farmer would not get compensation any more than the packer.

It is quite impossible to make an efficient inspection unless the inpsection takes place right when the animal is slaughtered. At all events, it seems to me the present condition is unfair to the packers, and the whole subject is one which should be properly considered. There is no question but that it is a matter which the Dominion might work out, possibly in co-operation with the provinces. But inspection for home consumption is not necessary, and it is a very invidious distinction that the people who consume our products in the foreign markets should be protected, and that Canadians should be left without protection. I may have eaten meat to-day which was not fit for food, but I am not in a position to know whether it was or not. Of course I escape that risk one day in the week, and as the Minister of Agriculture probably indulges in meat seven days in the week ho probably may be taking a greater risk than I do. However, I think there should be inspection of meat for home consumption. That shows that the man who buys for export buys the best meat he can get. He buys, if possible, superior meat to that bought by the man who slaughters and sells locally. It is not desirable that this should be. If inspection is good for for-' eigners, to whom we sell our meat, surely it is good for our own people. The whole
63!0

matter is one which I think should fully engage the attention of the government, with a view to devising some equitable law which might be worked out if necessary in co-operation with the provincial authorities.

I have listened to the discussion that has been going on for the last three hours upon this subject, and with many other hon. members I have come to the conclusion that the government should do something to meet a condition that is unfavourable, not only to the packer, but to the farmer as well. There i3 no doubt in my mind that if a proper inspection were made of all the meats in the packing houses, and if the government assumed a reasonable responsibility for the loss sustained by either the packer or the farmer they would be doing what the public expected them to do. I have no doubt that the minister is endeavouring to do the best he can under very difficult conditions, and I have been hoping that something would be arrived at to meet the conditions complained of by some hon. members to-day. I have felt, whether my judgment in the matter is right or not, that if there were a system of inspection and compensation, the packer would be able to pay to the farmer a better price for hogs or cattle than he is paying at the present time, although there is not much reason to complain of present prices. I have been in packing houses where I have been surprised at the large number of diseased animals that have had to be destroyed, and the meat of which has not been disposed of to the public for consumption, either for export or domestic use; and I have endeavoured to see whether it would not be possible to have these animals ear-marked, so to speak, so that it might be known from what drover or from what locality they came. While that might be possible, it would be very difficult. I hone that the Minister of Agriculture, who usually works out these problems in a satisfactory manner, will be able to devise seme method by which the packers shall be properly compensated for diseased animals ear-marked, so to speak, and destroyed in the public interest. In this event the buyer would be in a position to offer better prices since he would be assuming no risk of having his profits decreased by the possible destruction of diseased meat.

I agree largely with what the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) has said in regard to allowing compensation to packing concerns for diseased carcases or hogs or cattle; but the packing houses are not the only parties who should be considered in this matter. We have in the southwestern part of Ontario a large number of farmers who them-Mr. A. C. MACDONELL.
selves go quite extensively into the dressing of hogs. These dressed hogs are inspected by the government inspectors at the different shipping stations, and when a hog is found by a government officer to be wholly diseased, it is sent back to the farmer who is shipping it or is destroyed on the spot, and the farmer suffers the entire loss, not the packer or the buyer. So that if the government are considering the advisability of compensating the drover or the packer they should not overlook the farmer. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) found fault with the government for allowing interprovincial trade between some of the provinces in meat that has not passed government inspection. I may say that we in Ontario would like to have accorded to us the treatment which the hon. gentleman is objecting to for his particular province, that is, allowing it to trade in uninspected meat with Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, or some of the other provinces.
I did not say that we were allowed to do anything of the kind.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that an interprovincial trade that was not subject to government inspection was allowed between some of the provinces.
Between the three maritime provinces.

That is what I understood; and the very conditions which the hon. member for Halifax was finding fault with in this particular section of the country are the conditions which we would be glad to have in the province of Ontario, under which we could trade with the province of Quebec in our heavy carcases of dressed hogs without government inspection; and if the government continues to allow the maritime provinces the privilege in that respect which they are enjoying at the present time, I hope they will extend the same privilege to our province. If they do, I feel sure that their action will meet with general satisfaction. We do not ask for favours which other provinces are not getting; but if Nova Scotia is granted the privilege of sending its meat products without government inspection to other provinces, the producers and packing houses of the province of Ontario will be placed in an awkard position if they are not granted the same privilege. If the government consider the advisability of qom-pensating packing houses for the loss of diseased carcases, I hope they will also take into consideration the advisability of compensating the producer, who at present very often is obliged to lose carcases of dressed hogs which are rejected by the government inspectors.

What my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Maedonell) has said about the packers was most vigorously denied this morning by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), who stated that the packers did not suffer the loss, but that the drovers did. That is a matter I know nothing of; it ia a matter of private agreement between the packers and the drovers or between the drovers and the farmers. The different information given to this House this afternoon is a clear indication that we have not any decisive or accurate information to go upon. I want to say a word on the general question of compensation. If we once began to pay compensation for meat, not living animals, we would, as the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) says, have to pay compensation for any animal that any one might find diseased-the farmer, the butcher or the packer. If we do that we may be perfectly certain that hundreds of animals will be killed, and dressed which the owners who killed and dressed them knew perfectly well were not fit for human food. We will have to pay hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars for animals, which before they were killed would be known to be unfit for human food. I would be glad to pay compensation wherever it seemed justified, but I again point out that when we were discussing the payment of compensation for animals killed I was warned by hon, gentlemen opposite, and by some on this side that there was great danger of a large expenditure of money with no particular advantage to the public, and that we must be very careful to safeguard the public against that kind of thing. I would not like to propose an amendment to the Act providing for compensation of this kind without having some shrewd suspicion of what the cost would amount to. When asking for authority to pay compensation for animals slaughtered on account of disease I was able to estimate the probable cost, and I am jjlad to say that experience has shown that the estimate was fairly accurate. Losses of this kind in the case of dead meat should be arranged by private bargain between the buyer and seller. If we took authority to pay compensation for dead meat we should logically pay for fruit, vegetables, &c., condemned, and the cost would undoubtedly Teach half a million dollars which I am sure parliament would not endorse.

I have had some requests along the line of the discussion this afternoon. I think it is strange that men who come under the operation of this Inspection Act should be the entire losers of animals condemned when it is done to protect the trade of Canada for beef, and hogs. I do
not see why a man engaged in that line of business should be the entire loser. He is an innocent party just as the man who has live animals killed on account of disease. In that case you compensate to the extent of two-thirds the value of the live animals slaughtered to protect the public against disease, and there has been no complaint against the government compensating people who are unfortunate enough to own such animals. I do not see why you should not be prepared to compensate an innocent man for loss in the case of something that is done to protect the lives of people just as in the case of guarding against the spread of disease among live animals. The arguments in favour of compensation are even stronger. I think the country would be justified in paying the amount. I understand this question was laid before the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Agriculture last summer, and the government gave very favourable replies to those asking that such compensation should be provided for. As far as I am able to see, the minister is not making any provision for it in this Bill. It is also strange that wholesale dealers trading in, and slaughtering stock to be consumed by our own people are not brought under inspection to the same extent as men engaged in a larger business for export. One is as important as the other, and they should be treated alike. I would like to see the minister provide compensation for the man who suffers heavy loss in order that the trade of Canada may be protected, when he meets with this serious loss in an innocent way.

I did not rise to oppose the Act, but to try if possible to secure the removal of an interruption of trade brought about by certain conditions. My hon. friend from West Kent (Mr. McCoig) evidently misunderstood me. I did not state that we have an interprovincial trade. We may have, and I understand from. the minister that we have, but the province of Prince Edward Island sometimes sells products to merchants in Halifax ot may send them there for export. On that we have no complaint. The complaint I made if any was that the products of the slaughter house or meat preserving factory or canning factory were permitted to be sold to the local dealers, and those living in the province even if they were not fit for export. The minister says that the province ought to attend to that. The contention of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. A. C. Maedonell) is that if the power lies not with the Dominion government, but with the provincial government, and the provincial government does not make provision, it must reasonably fall to the Dominion government if there be an Act for food inspection to put

.it into operation wherever there does not .seem to be a local Act in force or else to ask the local government or authority to bring in such an Act. I am not contending about that, my contention is simply that we had an interruption of trade and commerce. The most beneficial trade is the export trade, and it should be properly guarded. My hon. friend will say that is why he has brought in this Act. Perhaps that is a good reason for having the Act. But here we have a trade and commerce that has been going on for many years, and the suspension of that trade might be delayed for two or three weeks in order to allow men in the export trade to have an opportunity to ship goods they have on hand. The people of the West Indies are ready to take these goods-, and to pay for them. I would like it distinctly understood that I am not complaining of the Act. It is all right to have the Act in force, and we do not ask for any treatment different from that given to everybody else. But, when there has been a delay in the enforcement of the law, apparently through somebody's neglect-not that I am trying to cast blame on anybody-I think it is only fair to allow those concerned a short time to adapt themselves to the new conditions under the law.
Does not the minister intend to strike out the word ' goats ' in this section? He might as well include dogs.
We know that goats are slaughtered, and, if a goat carcass should happen to come before us, with this word in the law, we could deal with it.
It is generally rumoured that dogs are slaughtered.
I do not believe that they are slaughtered for food purposes.
Does the minister intend to make clearer the definition of the word ' farmer '?
If m.y hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) would suggest a change, I will be glad to consider it. The clause was drafted by the law clerk and is supposed to be as good a definition as we can make.

Take the case of the hon. member for South York (Air. W. F. Maclean). He is a journalist to all intents and purposes, yet carrying on farming quite extensively, breeding, growing and fattening animals. But farming is not his recognized occupation. Would he come under this definition?

The hon. member (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is recognized as a journalist, but recognized also as a farmer. I am glad to say that farming is an occupation so attractive that many engage in it with their other occupations. But such people, 1 Mr. CROSBY.
think, are recognized as farmers. There are many members of this House who are engaged in other occupations, who yet claim the right to be considered farmers.
Mr. SPROLrLE. It speaks of ' his recognized occupation.' Can a man have two
recognized occupations at the same time under the law?
I think so.
I should feel surer of it if some eminent lawyer in the House endorsed that opinion.
It is quite a common thing in legal documents to have a man described of two occupations. I recall the case of a man being described as a ' farmer and mill-owner.'
, If this man should slaughter hogs, what would be hi-s occupation?
He is a farmer.

I am afraid that is one of these things we will have to let go; 1 do not think we will get anything that will exactly fill the bill.
On section 3,

This provides for the striking out of certain words in the existing law. The words to be struck out are ' animals slaughtered by retail butchers on their own premises.' This is a section which allows farmers to slaughter without an inspection. At first it was supposed that retail butchers might be included, but we have found that retail butchers have been entering into the wholesale trade while free from the provisions of the Act, and it is necessary that they should no longer have the privilege which was intended originally for farmers only. The striking out of these words will prevent retail butchers from exporting from one province to another without inspection.
The minister, I understand, has a law clerk in connection with his department, or'some person to draft a Bill?
We have left that to the Justice Department or to the law clerk of the House.

If that were the general practice of the House, I should be glad to follow it. But the custom is where the amendments are not long or important, to do the work in this way. The amendments in this case are almost wholly minor amendments. I think the one we have under discussion is the only one that affects any class of people directly; the others merely have the effect of making the administration of the law more easy.

But does the minister himself think that my plan would be better? The people in the country may not have the statutes. They send down here and ask the King's Printer for a copy of the Act, and instead of getting one they get two. Why do not the Department of Justice, and the law clerk of the House of Commons get together and once for all accomplish the whole thing? If it is not the usual practice, I think the minister could inaugurate a new system.
I will consult with the Justice Department about it.
Could the minister tell me what proportion of the cattle that are exported from Canada are inspected?
All live cattle that go across the water are inspected.
Why not those going to the United States?

The trade in live cattle to Great Britain is so much more important, and the British authorities are so particular about the landing of animals there we have to see that no animal affected in the slightest degree with disease is sent across the water. Unless we did that we might be shut out from their market.
At what points are export cattle inspected?
At different places, but they are finally inspected when they go on board iship. Those that go by United States ports from Canada to Great Bjitain are inspected in Canada.
Are we then to understand that it is impossible for an exporter to send cattle from Canada to the old country without a rigid inspection?

Quite so.
On section 12,

Thi3 section is practically the same as in the old Act, but it gives the authorities access to the books and bills
of lading of the firm, 30 as to be able to check their exports, and to see that everything they send out of their establishment has been inspected in accordance with the law.
On section 13,
I would suggest as the interpretation of the word ' farmer ', a person whose recognized occupation is farming, because he might be engaged in more than one occupation.

The intention of this clause is to prevent men who are dealers having the advantage of it. A dealer might have a little piece of ground and pretend to be a farmer. But still I would not think there was very much objection to the suggestion of my hon. friend.

It would be a rare thing for a man to occupy a small piece of ground and palm himself off as a farmer if in reality he was not doing the general work of a farmer in all lines. But, if a man is doing the usual work in all lines of a farmer he is entitled to be considered a3 a farmer.
I would not like to change it without consulting the law officers.
Could it not be left an open question while the minister consulted the law officers?
The Bill might go out of committee and on the third reading the amendment could be introduced.

That would be all right.
On the preamble,

I see that this Bill refers to canned goods. I have here a number of labels with reference to canned articles which are, to a certain extent, deceiving the public. I do not wish to present these labels to the House because there are a great many others probably of the same character, and it might affect individual firms who may he actually within the law. But I would ask the minister if he could not see his way clear, while this Bill is under consideration, to add something in reference to this matter. I have here a label which says: ' Unfermented native wine'. This is a label placed on goods which are being sold by a firm in Toronto and elsewhere for medicinal purposes. One would judge that the ingredients are the produce of the grape, but this is not so. Here is another:	'Fine domestic port.'
You would infer from that that this was manufactured from the juice of the grape for medicinal purposes. I merely suggest to the minister that something should be done to cover this point, and I would ask if he could not do it in connection with this

Bill. I would suggest that any article which is canned or bottled must bear a label declaring whether it is a mixture or a pure product, or whether, as in the case of these wines, it is from the grape or otherwise. Large quantities of these mixtures are being bought for use by the sick, I believe, under the impression they are juice of the grape. I would also projpose that the label on canned articles should bear the date of their manufacture. The label should specify exactly what is contained in the can, and the date at which the goods were canned, sc that the inspector would be able to form some idea as to the age of the goods.

Goods such as my hon. friend describes do not come under this Act at all. They would come under the Adulteration of Foods Act, which is under the administration of the Inland Revenue Department. I think that any such statement as that which my hon. friend has read from those labels w7,ould render the parties responsible for them liable to attack under the Adulteration of Foods Act, on the ground of misrepresentation. However, I would not like to give a legal opinion.
My remarks as to the age of canned articles would apply to this Act, would they not?
The question as to requiring the date to be placed on canned goods was discussed for a long time upon the introduction of this Bill and parliament decided against requiring it to be put on the cans.

Speaking earlier on this question I suggested to the minister the wisdom of making some amendment to the law or some provision with regard to labelling meats in cold storage and putting upon them the date on which they were placed in the cold storage. Has the minister considered that question? It seems that this is a very proper place to bring it in if he desires to do so. The information which we have justifies action by the government or parliament with reference to this very question. It is an evil that is perhaps much greater in its proportions than we are aware of, but what has been brought to our notice justifies some provision of law to compel the stamping of the date on the goods at which meats were put in cold storage, and also a provision as to the length of time it was held in cold storage before being disposed of.

I do not think that at the present time we have sufficient information to go upon to enable us to introduce any such legislation. I see a great deal of that subject in the press and I know that it is attracting a great deal of attention. But, I am prepared at the present moment to express a very positive opinion Mr. LEWIS.
upon it. I have always understood that some goods in cold storage might deteriorate while other goods might not. If some goods were kept in cold storage for a few months they might be unfit for human food while in another case they might be there for a year and be perfectly good. I do not know enough about it to express an opinion or to undertake to draft any legislation upon the subject. Whether such legislation ought to come in connection with this Bill or not I am not certain. It is of another character and yet perhaps it might come within the pur-vievv of such an Act as this. It is a large subject and I have not come to any conclusion upon it.

Is the subject not of sufficient importance to justify the minister in making careful inquiry in regard to it, because the allegations are so specific that if thej be true there is no doubt that it is one in which this parliament should act. Take, for instance, the statement in regard to the length of time that carcases have been held in cold storage; 2,000 carcases were held in cold storage in Montreal for two years. That is a specific statement which is capable of being verified or -disproved.
I do -not think that it is accompanied by the allegation that these carcases are unfit for use. They may be, or they may not be; I do'not know.

I do not say that it is, but I say as a medical man, that unless the temperature was kept absolutely below a given point and not allowed to go up and down, as it very frequently -does in cold storage places, that article would be unfit for food after a given time.
I think so.

But even though the quality of the article might not have been deteriorated to any extent, does the minister not think that the very fact that it is kept in cold storage for that length of time, during which foods are very dear and the public is prevented from using it and that it could only be held for one purpose and that is for the purpose of trying to control the market, would justify the passing of some law to prevent that being -done? Would the minister not think that that would be of sufficient importance to justify him in making some law to control that and to say that goods shall not be kept in cold storage beyond a reasonable times before being sold?

There are two points which my hon. friend has brought up and which are entirely different. One is as to whether food is fit for human consumption after a certain time. That is a question of public health and perhaps might come

under an Act such as this. The other is a question of affecting the market price. That is entirely apart from the question of whether food is fit for human consumption and that certainly -would not come under an Act in regard to the inspection of food. It is another question whether such legislation ought to be passed.

The inspection of food for export is for the benefit of our trade generally. If food is kept in cold storage for a few years and is then exported, has the minister any guarantee that the food is perfectly wholesome? The minister has a perfect right to deal with that class of exports.
On the question of quality, yes.
And as one object of cold storage is to enhance prices, could the minister not get at that practice under the Jaw which deals with restraint of trade and unduly enhancing prices?
Possibly, but that has nothing to do with this Act.	.

To my mind this is the proper place to put in a clause dealing with the abuses which exist in reference to cold storage.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
. GOVERNMENT ANNUITIES.
FIELDING moved the second reading of Bill (No 155) to amend the Government Annuities Act, 1908.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This Bill has been carried through the Senate by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and is designed to provide some improvements in the Government Annuities Act. which have been found to be necessary. The amendments are not very important, but they will help to make the system work more simply. One change is the provision that one may buy an annuity, not merely for himself, but for another. The law now provides that the purchaser of an annuity may contract for an annuity to himself, but it is desired that he may have the privilege to buy an annuity for another person. For example, a missionary society may desire to make provision for an annuity to a missionary, and there are many other cases of that character. Another amendment provides that a contract may be made for a fixed period; you not only make an arrangement for an annuity to a man during his lifetime, but you may make an arrangement that that annuity may be paid to some one for a fixed period, and if the annuitant dies in the meantime, the annuity may be continued to some other person designated by him.
Another provision is with reference to annuitants far advanced in life. At present, an annuity may be granted to a person above 80 years of age, but if he were 85 years old he would pay the same amount as the man 80 years old, whereas the former, of course, should get the cheaper rate. There is a provision in the existing law that the husband may convert a portion of his annuity for the benefit of his wife, and this amendment proposes that the wife shall have the same privilege of converting part of her annuity for the benefit of her husband.
What amount is in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The number of annuitants outstanding is 614, of which 374 are males and 270 females. The purchase money received to date is $483,359.44; the amount of the annuities represented by this payment is $160,500, and the average annuity $250.

Can you give that information by provinces?
AH. FIELDING. A statement to that effect could be prepared. Applications have come from every province in the Dominion, and from the Yukon.
Hqw many men are out soliciting annuities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are four men and one lady in Ontario, one in New Brunswick, one in Nova Scotia, two in Quebec, in all, 9 agents.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1.
I understand that annuities may be obtained through postmasters, but have you recognized agents who are paid a commission for soliciting annuitants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The agents are all paid salaries and travelling expenses, but the postmasters and other officials who send in business are paid a commission at the rate of one-third of one per cent on the amount of money which they collect or receive.
What officers are employed by the government at headquarters for managing this branch of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a return already before the House giving information in every detail. In the office at Ottawa there are twelve clerks.
What is about the gross expense here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From $12,000 to $15,000 is the expense of the salaries at Ottawa.
On section 2-purchaser defined,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The purpose of this is to enable a purchaser to provide an annuity not merely for himself, but for another person, as a father for a child. This broadens the definition of purchaser so as to cover that point.	.
How will this affect those who have already taken out annuities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There have been several contracts made that would come within the amendments, and section 9 makes thi3 Act apply to annuities entered into prior to the passing of this Act.
On section 3-sale of annuities authorized,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a re-enactment of the section. It is so worded as to make it clear that an annuity may be granted not merely for the life time of the annuitant, but for a definite period, so that the annuitant, in anticipation of death, might arrange that the annuity should pass to some other person for the term of the annuity.
Will a person now having an annuity under the original Act have a right to convert it under the proposed amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, if he deems it desirable.
On section 4-payments by purchaser,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This refers to contracts made by employers for the benefit of those in their service. The clause a3 it formerly stood rather restricted their freedom of contract. This broadens the arrangement and enables the employer to make any contract respecting an annuity which is satisfactory to himself and the person concerned.
'On section 9, application of the Act.
I understand there is no medical examination required in selling annuities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
There is no examination of the physical or mental condition of the individual.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that there is no medical examination for annuities. It is not thought necessary. Of course, if the annuitant is not in good health and dies at an early period, he and his estate are the sufferers.
But you have provision that in some cases after his death the annuity may go to some one else?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For a limited period. In regard to life insurance, medical examination is important, but in annuities, a medical examination is not deemed necessary.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

Mr. FISHER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 185) respecting the Commission for the Conservation of Natural Resources. He said: Only one or two small changes are proposed. One is to allow the annual meeting to be held in a different place than Ottawa. Another is that the chairman of a committee can summon a meeting of such committee at any time, and that when a committee is summoned members of the committee attending its meetings ^ may have their disbursements paid as in the case of the annual meetings. Another provision is to make mail matter addressed to the commission free of Canada postage.
I would ask title Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) whether he has taken into consideration the clauses that I suggested should be added to this measure.

I read carefullv the amendments proposed by the hon.' member (Mr. Armstrong). I have thought that something of the kind he suggests might be quite proper, but I fear that amendments as proposed by the hon. gentleman would have the practical effect of making such a commission as this impossible. His proposals are so drastic that I am sure nobody would accept a position on the, commission to be hampered in his private business in the way these amendments would make inevitable. It is well worthy of consideration whether some such amendments might not be properly adopted, but I confess that I have not had time or opportunity-nor has the chairman of the commission-to draw up amendments that would be proper, and feasible, and practicable. I am not- prepared to give a legal opinion concerning the amendments proposed, but I am under the impression that, if they were passed, no member of the commission could hold stock in a mine; I doubt if any could hold stock in a railway company. I fear that the amendments proposed are of such a character as to be entirely unworkable.

I am afraid the Minister of Agriculture has not investigated the matter or he would have found the opposite of what he has stated. Of the amendments I have suggested to this Bill, one

is taken from clause 14 of the Geological Survey Act-which seems to be a workable Act-and the other from clause 376 of the Railway Act. These clauses are practically embodied in the amendments I have suggested. When the minister says they would have the effect of prohibiting a member of the commission from undertaking any work of his own, I do not see that anything of that kind is indicated. The position is simply this:	At present, the
door is wide open so far as these commissioners are concerned. The commissioners can expend any quantity of public money in developing certain resources of this country, investigating mines or timber tracts, and they can then make these their own practically, and without any one to forbid them. But if the amendments I propose were embodied in this measure, there would be no further trouble in that regard. I sincerely hope that the minister will see the wisdom of the position taken in regard to this matter, and will embody these provisions in the Bill.

The question which my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) has brought before the House is undoubtedly an important one. If the commission of conservation is to serve a useful purpose for the people of Canada, the law relating to it must be of such a character as will give both Houses of parliament, and the people generally full confidence that the commission will not be made use of for any improper purpose. The idea which apparently runs through the Act constituting the commission, and which must be taken to express the mind of parliament upon the subject, was that men of affairs should be induced to act upon this commission gratuitously, and give the benefit of their judgment, and experience in the public interest. Every one will admit that the usefulness of the commission would be gone at once if there was the slightest suspicion, or could be the slightest suspicion, that any information which was gained or collected by the commission would be used, or is likely to be used, for any private purposes. But, let me point out to my hon. friend that the provisions of the laws which he has incorporated in his Bill are provisions which relate to branches of the Civil Service, they govern the employment of men who are technical employees of the government, who are paid a salary by the government which compensates them for their whole time, and the condition of their entering the services of the government in these classes of work is that no other business or calling shall be followed, and therefore, it is an easy matter to provide that these employees shall not make use of information to make investments which information has been secured in the course of their official employment. But the members of 'the commission of conservation are not civil servants or salaried employees of the government; they are business men, a considerable number of whom are engaged in affairs in a large way, and to whom the application of such a rule would be absolutely impossible. Let me give an illustration. ' Senator W. C. Edwards is chairman of the committee on forestry, and is giving a considerable portion of time to the work of the commission. He is recognized by everybody as an able, and experienced business man, a man very well qualified to do what he is doing, and to lender valuable public service, a man), moreover, whose time is extremely valuable, and who if he gives his time to the public service does so at a very considerable financial sacrifice. Senator Edwards is a lumberman. If I read the hon. member's (Mr. Armstrong's) amendment aright, Senator Edwards could not buy another timber limit, and remain a member of the commission.
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is chairman of the Committee on Public Health. He has been giving a good deal of careful consideration to the important branch of the work which he has undertaken to supervise. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) is a director of the Canadian Pacific railway, and I think, a large stockholder. The Canadian Pacific railway deals in natural resources-mines water-powers, and so on-on a very extensive scale. I doubt that Air. Osier could buy another share of Canadian Pacific railway stock without making himself liable under the provisions of the Act. My hon. friend must remember that provisions of this kind, drawn in general terms, are very far-reaching. There is no difference of opinion between the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) and the minister in charge of the Bill, or mvself, or, I imagine, any member of the commission. What we would desire, and I think what we would insist on, will be that the law must be in a condition that is satisfactory to parliament. I would not, speaking for myself, remain in the position of chairman of the commission for a minute if I thought that the sentiment of parliament on the other side of the House was that the law was not in a perfectly satisfactory condition, or that the House generally was not satisfied with the condition of the law. Certainly, I do not think the members of the commission would hold their offices under a statute which was forced through by a government majority against the "wishes of the members of the opposition. That would be entirely contrary to the spirit in which the commission is organized, and in which, so far, it has been, very happily, carried on.
I would make a suggestion to my hon. friend the minister. I am speaking as a 1 lawyer who has had some experience :n

drawing statutes of various kinds, and I think you will find it very difficult to draw a provision which, when thoroughly considered, will prove to be satisfactory in regard to a matter of this kind. It will take a good deal of time and discussion, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that he, and perhaps the leader of the opposition, and the minister who has charge of the Bill, and myself, with perhaps one or two members of the commission, should get together and discuss the matter, and see if we can work out a provision which will be satisfactory; omit it can be fully and carefully considered, and brought in at the next session of parliament, and made a portion of the law. I do not think that the object can be attained without very careful consideration. I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) himself, would like to enforce an amendment which would have the effect of making the members of the commission feel that it was not safe for them to continue their ordinary business. In such a case as that they would simply resign from the commission, and a work which has been happily commenced, and with an augury of a considerable amount of good to the public, would be practically destroyed.

I wish to say distinctly I had no other object in view in bringing forward this measure than to promote the public welfare. I would like the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) be good enough to tell us whether he thinks that the present measure safeguards the people's interest sufficiently, and what suggestions he would make.

I do not know exactly what my hon. friend means. There is no provision in the Act as it stands at present which in any way relates to what the members of the commission may do or may not do. They are appointed as a non-salaried body for the purpose of doing an important * public work. There are two ways of dealing with them. One way is for the House to put them on their honour and not make any legal provision at all; the other way is to make some provision of law which shall act as a deterrent to any person who might be disposed to do that which is contrary to the public interest. It will be for the House to decide which method they desire to follow. I would not say that the public interest is not protected simply because there is nothing in the statute which prevents the members of the commission from making use of their public position for their private ends.

I asked the Minister of Agriculture the other day if he would tell the House under what circumstances and in what way communications could be interchanged with, or advice ob-Mr. SIFTON.
tained from, this commission in regard to Bills that came before any committees of this House involving the great natural resources of the country; and the minister thought he would be in a position to do something when this measure came up. For instance, in the Railway Committee on several occasions the waterways question has come up, and we did not know in what way to proceed in order to get the advice of this commission. I think some system ought to be arranged whereby that can be done.

Of course this commission is a new thing, and the scope of its work, while fairly defined in the Bill, is still subject to practical experience. I understand that on one or two occasions during this session committees have asked for information or advice from the commission. I do not suppose that we would want to restrict the committees of the House from doing anything which they thought in the public interest. I can understand that it would be advisable, before the course of action proceeds much further, if it is going to be proceeded with at all, that some general line of action should be laid down. Just what that line of action should be I am not prepared to say. Perhaps it would be well for the committee of the House who strike all the committees, to consult with the executive committee of the commission, or the chairmen of the different committees of the House to consult with the chairman of the commission, and thus gradually to work out a scheme by means of which communications may pass between either House and the committees of the House, and the commission. I can understand that in the working out of a thing of this kind action may be taken by one body a little different from action taken by another body; one committee of the House may proceed in one way and another committee in another way, and this is an additional proof of the necessity of taking steps to see that a general line of procedure is laid down. I think before the next session of parliament something of the kind ought to be done, or at any rate, in the early days of next session, if the consensus of opinion in the House is that the commission should be consulted, that there should be established some means of communication between the House and the commission.
What we want is that committees of the House may have access to the advice of the commission, and to the statistics and information which the commission have collected.

I think one of the defects of the commission Bill is that they must report to the Governor in Counpil. It is true that they are appointed under statute, but I never could see the reason why they should not make their report to

parliament instead of to the Governor in Council, and then every member of parliament would have an opportunity of perusing their report. It may be presented to the Governor in Council, and I think there is some provision that it is to be laid before the House, but I am not sure. I think it ought to be presented to parliament, and then the Governor in Council might be the Intermediary between committees of the House and this commission. When we were dealing with a Bill last night, I asked the question whether this committee had considered it, and what report they had made on it, and I was told by the Minister of Public Works that they had it under consideration. But I got no information as to how long it had been under consideration, or what their views on it were. That leaves the commission practically worthless to parliament.
Their report has to be laid on the table of parliament immediately it is made.

The idea of my hon. friend is perfectly correct, that is to say, the idea that the commission is not a portion of the administrative machinery of the government, or a political body, but it is directly, or indirectly responsible to the House as a non-partisan body. There must be some way of getting their report before the House of Commons, and under our system of government there is no other way except for them to present their report to the Governor in Council, and he to transmit it to parliament unless it should be done _ through Mr. Speaker. My hon. friend will see that the section in the original Bill is that the commission should make its report to the Governor in Council at the end of the fiscal year, and the Governor in Council should lay it before parliament. There is no other way in which it can be got before parliament. The method of sending it to the Governor General in Council, and having it transmitted to parliament, seems the most convenient one.
Is there not a department which is the intermediary between the House and the commission?
Yes.

Then could the report not be made to the department and laid before parliament, instead of being made to the Governor in Council? The defect in it, to my mind, is that what might be given to the Governor General in Council might not be available for parliament. Section 13 provides that:
The commission shall make its report to the Governor General in Council at the end of each fiscal year, and such report shall be printed and laid before both Houses of parliament.
But we have current work going on, Bills before the Railway and Private Bills Committees, and there questions relating to the work of the commission, regarding which we desire to get the views of the commission who are clothed with authority to look into these questions at any time, and give the Governor in Council, or parliament the benefit of their knowledge, or inquiry. Between one session and another, all that work may be done, but parliament cannot avail itself of the benefits of that work for the current labours that are going on during the session until the end of the year, or until the beginning of the next session when the information is practically out of date as far as its requirements go, and when it is not likely to turn back and make a beneficial use of it.

Before proceeding with the measure, I would like to know whether, it is not possible to have these clauses placed in the Bill. I have gone to a great deal of trouble over this matter; I made a thorough investigation from a lawyer's standpoint. I am satisfied that the clauses are reasonable, and I have no thought of objecting to the position taken by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-ton) in particular any further than that he cannot give us any good reason why they should not be placed in the Bill. The clauses read as follows:
14. No member of the commission or persons appointed as secretary or as officers or clerks under him, or person employed as an assistant for the purpose of any special work or investigation, shall, while a member of the commission or appointed or employed as aforesaid-
(a) Purchase, lease, acquire or obtain, on royalty or otherwise, any Dominion or provincial franchises, fishery rights, water-powers, water privileges, lands, mines, mineral lands or timber limits, or in any way contract therefor or acquire any interest therein, either for himself or as agent for any other person or corporation.
While this might appear to interfere to some extent with the members of the commission, yet 1 can readily say to the hon. member for Brandon that as far as interfering with the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is concerned, if he will refer to clause 376 of the Railway Act he will find these words:
Every railway director of a railway company who knowingly permits the funds of any such company to be applied either directly or indirectly in the purchase of its own stock, or in the acquisition of any shares, bonds or other securities issued by any other railway company in Canada, or in the purchase or ac-

quisition of any interest in any such stock, shares, bonds or other securities, contrary to the provisions of this Act, shall incur a penalty of one thousand dollars for each such violation.
The penalty in the Bill that I suggested reads as follows:
Every person guilty of any violation of any provision in section 14 of this Act shall forfeit to His Majesty all property or interest so acquired or obtained, and shall also incur a penalty of $1,000 for each such violation.
Largely the same wording -as that which appears in clause 376 of the Railway Act, while the first clause I read compares with clause 14 of the Geological Survey Act, which is as follows:
No person employed in or under the department shall-
(a)	Purchase any Dominion or provincial lands except under authority of the Governor in Council.
(b)	Locate military or bounty land warrants, or land scrip, or act as agent of any other person m such behalf.
If I read that aright, it includes the minister who has charge of the department, and if it includes the minister, why not include the members of the Conservation Commission? It further reads:
(c)	Disclose to any person, except his superior officer, any discovery made by him or by any other officer of the department, or any other information in his possession in relation to matters under the control of the department or in relation to Dominion or provincial lands, until such discovery or inhas been reported to the minister, and his permission for such disclosure has been obtained.
(d)	Make investigations or reports relating to the value of the property of individuals, or hold any pecuniary interest, direct or indirect, in any mine, mineral lands, mining works or timber limits in Canada.
The hon. member for Brandon said that these are largely officials in the Geological Survey of Canada, but the hon. member for Brandon, -as chairman of the commission, will employ a large number of officials, and as this Act only permits them to be employed for a short space of time, they are more likely to dispose of the information that they obtain for an amount of money than are the members of the Geological Survey, who are in the employ of the government. I -am satisfied that if the Minister of Agriculture will take this into consideration he will readily see that there should be some clause which will at least control the men who are employed by this commission. At the present time members of the commission can have any -amount of money expended in investigating water-powers, mineral lands, or woodlands, and they can make these properties their own after having taken the people's money to thoroughly investigate them. Officers em-

ployed by this commission can do likewise. They can make discoveries and dispose of these discoveries, and there is no law to prevent them from acting in that way. A member of this commission has- a great advantage over the ordinary citizen. I am not reflecting on any member of this commission ; far from it, because a great many members of the commission are personal friends of my own, but I do think that they would be only too glad to have some such clause as the one that- I have referred to in the Act, so that there would be a guarantee that as far as the members of the commission and those employed by the commission were concerned, such proceedings as those which I have referred to would be impossible. I, therefore, trust that the minister will see his way to embody in the Bill the clauses which I have brought to his attention.

The most important clause in my hon. friend's amendment is subsection (a), the effect of which is to prohibit any member of the commission, or any person appointed by the commission, from engaging in the:
(a) Purchase, lease, acquire or obtain, on royalty or otherwise, any Dominion or provincial franchises, fishery rights, water-powers, water privileges, lands, mines, mineral lands or timber limits, or in any way contract therefor- or acquire any interest therein, either for himself or as agent for any other person or corporation.
I think that it is very possible, looking at it from a legal point of view, if that were passed that as a member of that commission I would not be safe in buying a share of Canadian Pacific railway stock. The Canadian Pacific railway traffics in public franchises dealing with a number of these things, and my own judgment is that by buying that stock I would be acquiring an interest in it. Another member of the commission is a director of the Canadian Pacific railway and a very large shareholder, and possibly deals in the stock of the company, and he would be debarred. Senator Edwards is a large lumber man and he buys timber limits, and he would be shut out from the commission. If the hon. gentleman is desirous to put the law in such a way that men of affairs who are doing business extensively cannot be members of the commission, it is for parliament to say whether that shall be so or not. For myself, as chairman of the commission, I do not think this is a matter I should be called upon to discuss, and I do not intend to discuss it in the sense of expressing my opinion as to what parliament ought to do. I simply point out to my hon. friend the effect his legislation would have upon the commission at the present time. If parliament thinks that they cannot trust the commission as it

stands, upon its honour, or that the law. should be such as would prevent men of the standing to whom I have referred, continuing membership on the commission, it is for parliament to say. It is not for us as members of the commission in this House to discuss what should be done. When you decide what you will do, then it will be for us to decide what we will do.

This commission must necessarily employ a number of officials who will visit remote localities and gather data regarding timber limits, water-powers, mines and other resources. These employees seem to be under no restraint so far as the law is concerned, and they may at any time sell in advance the information they acquire without fear of punishment, unless there be something in the Civil Service Act which would provide for that. The employees of this branch of the service seem to be exempt from the penalties for wrong-doing which other civil servants are subject to. I can quite understand the embarrassment there would be in dealing with the commissioners, and that it is possible they would have to be left entirely to their own honour, but I do not think the same should apply to the employees of the commission. We have heard over and over again that subordinates have given out information which has been taken advantage of by their friends and themselves to make a great deal of money. In the case, however, of employees of this commission there is no provision to punish any one who may give out information when he should not do so.

The contention of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) seems reasonable, and I think, perhaps, that the employees of this commission should be restricted in the same way as the employees of the geological survey. I will consult with the member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) to see if we cannot draw up an amendment which would embody the idea of the hon. gentleman with regard to the salaried officers of the commission.
