I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works if the government have any correspondence from the Hydro-Electric Commission of the province of Ontario in respect to this Bill?
There has certainly been none with me, and I am not aware of there being any correspondence with any other member of the government, although it is possible that there may have been.

Is it not rather important that the minister having charge of this Bill should place before the committee any such correspondence that may have taken place? As my hon. friend is aware, the government of Ontario are protecting, the rivers and streams in every part of the province for the people, and we accept with pleasure what the government stated last night by the Prime Minister, that the opposition were opposing this Bill because we were trying to impress upon this House and the country that we were in favour of a monopoly, I presume by the HydroElectric Commission of the province of Ontario. For myself I- am in favour of that kind of a monopoly. It differs entirely from the monopolies which lion, gentlemen opposite sometimes deal with in this House. The monopoly of the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario is the people of Ontario protecting their own, rights against all who would interfere with those rights, in taking possession of any ivaterway and manipulating it for private advantage. The government of Ontario are protecting all these streams, keeping in view the future development of electricity and the importance of cheap power for manufacturing; and, therefore, I think it .is not unfair that this committee should be put in possession of whatever correspondence there may have been between the Ontario government and this government, or between the Hvdro-Electric Commission and this government on this subject. I would have thought that the hon. Minister of Public Works would have been sufficiently interested in this matter to have inquired of the government if there was any such correspondence. I Avould have thought that my hon. friend would have been very anxious to communicate to this committee all correspondence that has come to the government or to any department of the government relative to this Bill, which has received so much attention in this House, and a greater amount of attention in the country, from the people of Ontario in particular. For myself, I want to go on record as being in opposition to any monopoly in this country.
Except that of the Hydro-Electric Commission.
Yes, I am fully in accord with that kind of a monopoly. It may be a kind of monopoly which my hon. friend, knows nothing about.
I am opposed to any monopoly.
Then there is a great opportunity for my hon. friend now, while this Bill is under discussion, to stand up and say that he is opposed to this monopoly.
I do not see that there is any monopoly in this.

My hon. friend is very quick to recognize what he calls a monopoly in the province of Ontario, which is a monopoly of the people for themselves. I think this government should be the first to commend the government of Ontario for rising in their might and saying to any class of people, whether they belong to the province of Ontario or to any other province, or whether they come from the United States or any other country, whether they be Liberal or Conservative, that their policy is a clearly-defined policy, that every water-power and every other public utility shall be protected for all the people of the province. If the Minister of Public Works thinks that I am a monopolist of that kind, I am willing to accept that, -and would only hope that I might be able to convert my hon. friend to that view. I would rather believe in the man who would correct his own government, his own department and his own policy, than cast reflections on the nolicy of the Ontario government with resoect to the Hydro-Electric Commission. I shall await now for my hon. friend to place before this committee to-night whatever correspondence the government or any department thereof has had either from the Ontario government of the Hydro-Electric Commission with respect to this Bill.

Before the Minister of Public Works makes his deliverance in answer to the hon. member, for Peel, may T ask him if he has ever considered the advisability of establishing a Hydro-Electric Commission under the auspices of the Public Works Department of the Dominion government, seeing that he is so much opposed to the one in the pmvince of Ontario?

I am rather surprised at my hon. friend from Peel being so unreasonable as he is. He seems to take for granted that late on in the evening, after business hours, after the public offices are all closed, that is the appropriate time at which to ask for papers, and he wants them delivered not to-morrow, not next Friday evening, but to-night.
We will wait until Friday.

I may say to my hon. friend that it is not at all convenient for me to send around to the offices to-night, after they are closed, to find out whether or not there is certain correspondence on file. But I may say to my hon. friend that I have not heard of either the HydroElectric Commission or the government of Ontario sending any communication to this government with reference to the Bill that is now before this committee.
It sent a representative before the committee.
That representative has been heard. Does my hon. friend say that he is on file and that I should get him and produce him to-night? I cannot do that.

May I be permitted to say that such a statement would be a very good argument if my hon. friend were introducing this Bill for the first time; but when my hon. friend remembers that this Bill has been before the House and the country for many weeks, and that he took part in an all-night discussion upon it, it might occur to him that it would be his duty to see that whatever information was in his department or in the possession of the government of which he is a prominent member should be laid before this committee for use in the discussion of this Bill.

I would rather assume that since the Bill has been so long before the House there is no correspondence or I would have heard of it. And I would assume that my hon. friend, who poses here as the champion of the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, and who has the courage to declare himself absolutely in favour of a monopoly so far as the transmission of electrical energy throughout the province of Ontario is concerned, who is strenuously opposed to the people being permitted to purchase electrical energy from any other person or body than the Hydro-Electric Commission, would have been the very first to be made acquainted of any correspondence by his friends of the commission, and the fact of his not being aware of any correspondence and of no correspondence coming to my notice, may, I think, be taken as very good evidence that there has been no correspondence. I take it for granted that the Hydro-Electric Commission, for reasons of its own, preferred to send counsel to appear before the Private Bills Committee to present their views. The hon. gentleman has also unwittingly fallen into an error of another description. He has stated that the Minister of Public Works is in charge of this Bill. My hon. friend surely cannot have forgotten that it has been stated over and over again that this is not a government measure, that

neither I nor any other member of the government is in charge of this Bill.
Does my hon. friend disown it?

It is impossible to disown what one never possessed. I have a duty to discharge just as my hon. friends have, and, when the Bill introduced as it was hy a private member, came before the committee for consideration, it was my duty to take the view of the matter which seemed to me to be the proper view to take.

Does my hon. friend wish to draw a distinction between the gentleman having charge of this Bill and the government, the cabinet? If my hon. friend does, the committee would be very glad to hear him state whether he himself and his government are in favour of or opposed to this Bill.

I can only speak for myself. I have not the slightest idea as to the views of the members of the government, except as they have been expressed on the floor of the House while.in committee. Every member of the government is free to vote as he pleases and, unlike the gentlemen on the other side of the House under the admirable leadersip which seems to be now prevailing and which excites the wonder and the astonishment of this country, every member on this side of the House is just as free to vote for or against the Bill as every member of the government is.,
How will they vote?

I am not able to say, but I will tell you how' I propose to vote. I propose voting for the Bill. While the Bill has been under discussion, I have been lost in amazement at the wonderful ingenuity of hon. gentlemen opposite in persuading themselves that there is something wrong or suspicious about this Bill, and that in some way it is connected with a Bill for the development of power on the St. Lawrence.

Then why did you
amend it?

We proposed to amend it for the very reason which the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) proposed an amendment which I have no doubt he had reason to believe would be unanimously accepted by his supporters; we amended it in order to make assurance 202 -
doubly sure, in order to make it impossible for any member of this House, or any person outside of this House to argue that the Bill was in any way connected with the damming of the St. Lawrence river. That is the question.

I am absolutely certain of it.

What the minister did say in effect was this: that he would not recommend to the Governor in Council that this Bill should go into effect until the plans and specifications had been approved. I have read the petition, the petition is from the Long Sault Development Company from the St. Lawrence Power Company and the Minister has said that this Bill shall not become operative until the plans of these two companies -and they both signed the petition, they are the same company-the minister says this Bill shall not come into force until these plans have been prepared and approved, and at the same time he says this company may get electricity transmitted over its lines from some other source, when the Bill itself would not come into force until he approves the plans of the other two companies. In the face of that, the minister says that he has a suspicion that the electricity which is going to pass over the transmission lines will come from the St. Lawrence Power Company, although that company does not come into operation until the plans are approved by himself.

I stated to the committee that I had not any knowledge whatever of what was in the mind of the promoters of this Bill we were all discussing. Its

terms were quite as new to me as they were to many other hon. members of this House. It stops there, and my hon. friend did not read that which, I say, qualifies entirely the remarks which I made. I said that I would answer some question which was put to me by my hon. friend from Westmorland.
I will answer as best I can. I do not know what is in the minds of the promoters of the Bill.
That is what I stated distinctly, and I did not know.

May I ask the Minister of Public Works now if that information which he gave was incorrect, namely, that the Bill will not go into force until the plans and specifications of the St. Lawrence Power Development Company and the Long Sault Development Company, now before the House, have been approved by the Governor General in Council?

I will say to my hon. friend that my own view is that if this Bill passes the Governor in Council would properly bring it into force entirely irrespective of any other company, or any other power development.
tain gentlemen representing a company appeared before council, and I ask the minister to submit the names to the committee as he has made reference to them. It would seem to me that it would be the proper thing to do.
I have no objection tu submitting such names as I can remember. I remember Mr. Leighton McCarthy, of Toronto, and a very eminent engineer-I forget his name.
Mr. Breakey?
I do not remember the name. Mr. Holgate, of Montreal, was before the committee of council, I think Mr. McGuigan, was there also, and some other gentlemen, but I do not remember their names.

I do not know.
Can the minister inform us whether or not the power which is now being developed by the St. Lawrence Power Company is being transmitted anywhere?
Then you must have given incorrect information before.

When I made the remarks which I did make in the House, the matter had not come before the council, and I could not speak for council, or profess to speak for council. I was entirely in the dark as to what the views of the promoters were, but I cannot see the slightest reason why this Bill should not be brought into force entirely irrespective of any other Bill. It has nothing to do with any other measure, and it would be brought into force on its own merits and with the view of transmitting power from any source from which the company might be able to obtain it.

Of this Bill?

Of the St. Lawrence Power Bill?
Mr. PUpSLEY. Yes, several persons on behalf of the company appeared before a sub-committee of council and asked for the approval of their plans. It was these plans which were submitted to the International Waterways Commission.

While I am on my feet I would like to put the situation very plainly before the House and the country. I do not believe there is an hon. gentleman in front of me but understands it thoroughly.
I think we do, and if we do it is bad for you.
I think the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) might be excused for not knowing anything about it.
If we do understand it it speaks very badly for the Minister and his party.

The minister and his party will always come out fairly well, if it he put on that basis, because my hon, friend is not quick at understanding things when he does not want to understand them. It is pretty near nine o'clock, and I want to say what I have to say before Mr. Chairman calls nine o'clock. The hon. members for Peel and North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) made it very plain that they were arguing largely because this was an interference with the hydro-electric plan. The hon. member for Peel devoted his remarks to that one point. On the other hand, the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) says that he objects to it because they are going to 'dam the St. Lawrence. I want the country to thoroughly understand my position. What I ask for, as representing the constituency of Brockville, is that we should be given the right to get cheap power if we can get it, no matter from what source. 'The people want-I care not wnat my hon. friends say-the cheapest power that they can get. It does not make any difference whether it comes from one company or another, or from the Hydro-Electric Commission, and the man who says that it must come from only one source is not a friend of the people.
Does it make any difference whether it interieres with the navigation of the St. Lawrence?

It is all very well for hon. gentlemen who are within a stone's throw of Niagara power and who are not in the position of having to seek for cheap power although when it does not come with that rapidity that was expected. They speak strongly in favour of the HydroElectric Commission only. The HydroElectric Commission has not yet come into that part of Ontario, no matter what is said to the contrary, and it has made no Mr. HUGHES.
serious attempt to come. No provision has been made in the estimates of the Ontario legislature for their coming. It is a delusion and a snare as far as the people of that part of the country are concerned. I have had some experience of this matter, and. I know of what I speak. If the Dominion has a power to lease to anybody, if it has a power to develop, these hon. gentlemen propose to take the ground that we must not give any person any right to transmit that power without going to the Ontario government and asking permission.
Why not run your own hydro-electric?

For my part, I believe that the policy adopted by this House unanimously in appointing a board of railway commissioners to control the rates on railways has been a success. I believe that that board can control the rates for power developed in the Dominion just as well as they can control railway rates, and with just as good results. If they give us as good results with respect to electrical power as they have with respect to the railways, the people of Canada will be the gainers. All we ask is that the right be given to a company to transmit power, get it where they may. There is nothing in this Bill, and hon. gentlemen know it perfectly well, to enable any person to dam the St. Lawrence. That is a big question that would have to be discussed in another spirit altogether. It is not contained in this Bill. If it were, I would not now ask this House to pass it.
Is there anything in this Bill that will strengthen the hands of the St. Lawrence Power Company and allow them to transmit electricity?

There is nothing in the Bill that will enable any company to dam the St. Lawrence, and the Bill further states in the amendment that they cannot add to the works heretofore constructed. They are confined absolutely to the works under construction. My hon. friend is trying to prevent me from saying what I wish to say before nine o'clock. I want to put the case plainly, because I want the country to understand it, a'nd I want my constituents to understand it, and I say that every member of this House does understand it. We ask for a transmission line, and whether or not they ever get power to dam the river St. Lawrence has nothing whatever to do with it. I have taken great pains to tell the promoters that I would not, in this Bill at least, have anything to do with a scheme which would enable them to1 get any more power than they had already on the St. Lawrence river.
Did they propose it?
My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) has many a time proposed things that he did not get, and it is a good thing for himself that he did not get them.

speechtext: A question can only be asked with the permission of the member who has the floor.
Well, I am asking him.

It is three or four minutes to nine o'clock, and I want to make my statement, and my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) is doing all he can to prevent me, but he can't. The House understands it, but I want to make it clear to the country and to my constituents who may not understand it. What we ask is that this company be given power to transmit power if there be any surplus now at Cornwall. I may be wrong, but I believe there is. There is a power at Iroquois owned by Mr. Beach not leased by the Ontario government, but leased to him by this government; there is a power at Waddington, opposite Morris-burg, that is to be developed, or that can be developed, and from which I am told we can get power to the town of Brockville; then there is another power at Messena, owned by this company or some of the same gentlemen who are in this company. We believe there is a surplus of power now, and if we cannot get any power from any of these works I mentioned, then no harm is done. But I say it is not fair; it is particularly not fair for the men from western Canada who have cheap power at their door to prevent us in the east getting the power which is running to waste and which I believe we can get if this company gets its charter.
It does.

All that is asked for by this Bill is that we be allowed in my constituency and elsewhere to utilize, through the means of this company being allowed to transmit it, the power that is going to waste. It makes no difference who is in the company; their powers are curtailed absolutely in this Bill, and though these men may be in the company to-day, if they do not see fit to go on with the work, the charter is in existence and I believe we can get men of capital to take that charter and give us a transmission line and give us the power we can obtain from these other
points. I again appeal to the House. We want power in the vicinity from which I come. I believe it would be absolutely unfair if this House should prevent us from getting the means of having that power brought to our doors. I say again that it is particularly unfair for those members who come from a section of this province, where the whole province is assessed them cheap power, that they should prevent us in the east from getting power when we are not asking the province to guarantee a single dollar to pay for it.

I call attention to the fact that in the papers brought down by the Minister of Public Works, we have the statement made in the petition which appears amongst these papers, that the St. Lawrence Power Company has 3,000 developed horse-power and 2,500 intermittent horse-power, which means that at certain seasons of the year they can develop 5,500 horse-power, and they have a capacity for developing 6,000 regular horse-power. Now, out of this quantity they state that there is only 1,000 or 1,500 horse-power used out of the 6,000 horse-power capable of development. In that same Bill this same company is given the right to sell and transmit that power, so that if the only question raised here is the getting of competitive power against the Hydro-Electric Commission, as stated by the Minister of Railways, they already have that power developed, they have the right to transmit it, they have the right to sell it, they have the right to supply it in competition with any other company at this very moment. That being the statement in the papers brought down by the Minister of Public Works, I cannot see why, under the circumstances, we could not take time to see the exact standing of this company without doing any injury either to the constituents of the Minister of Railways or to his portion of eastern Ontario of which he has spoken. I admire the position he took in fighting on behalf of the people of eastern Ontario, and I believe that if we can reduce the price of power by bringing in competition we should do so.
Hear, hear.

But I say his case is not sound because of the fact that he himself has already stated that that company has certain horse-power developed, and that all they require i3 that they may be able to transmit it to the localities that require it. As has been shown, under the section 8 of the Act of 1901, they have full power to do that, and that being the only reason advanced by the Minister of Railways why he is in favour of this Bill his contention falls to the ground. When

we take into consideration that the chairman of the Conservation Commission has reported absolutely against the Bill, and in view of all that has been said here, I venture to say that the Minister of Public Works is the only man in this House who has not yet become acquainted with the fact that the very same men who have asked for this Bill are the men who have control of the St. Lawrence Power Bill of 1901.

For lighting and for use at the locks. I understand there is only between thirty-five and sixty-five horse-power used on the canal, and I would like to have a statement from the officials as to the exact quantity used.

On section 4, payment of disbursements of members attending committee meetings.

Under the original Act it |
is provided that members shall be paid their disbursements in attending meetings of the commission. This follows out the same idea.
Why was not this provision put in the original Bill?

When the Bill was passed there were no committees, but, at the annual meeting, the organization of the commission was perfected by forming some committees, each to deal with its -own subject. This section is only carrying out the original idea by providing that the members shall have the same privileges when attending committee meetings as in attending meetings of the commission.

When the Act was drawn, the plan of work had not been fully thought out, and when the meeting was held we had to address ourselves to the question of how we were to conduct the work of the commission. The Act provided for the appointment of a chairman to be the executive officer of the commission. A difficulty that arose in connection with the practical work was that if the members of the commission met at the annual meeting, and passed general directions as to what should be done, thereafter the initiative would be left in the hands of the chairman, and the work and responsibility would devolve upon him. It was felt that that was not a desirable way to carry on the work. We desire to have the services of as many members of the commission as possible, and to have their judgment, and advice from time to time upon the various important questions with which we have to deal. After 'giving the matter the best consideration we could, we came to the conclusion that the best method of organization was Mr. LANCASTER.
to appoint committees to deal with the different classes of subjects, and to appoint a member of the commission as chairman of each committee. The logical corollary of that is that, from time to time, we shall be able to have meetings of the committees to discuss and deal with the particular subjects which these committees have in their purview. It will be seen that this will obviate the necessity of having more frequent meetings of the commission. Had this not been done, it would have been necessary to call meetings of the commission three or four times a year which would have meant bringing all the members of the commission here, and holding a large meeting when a small meeting might be all that is necessary. Under this scheme of organization, the practical work will be carried on by these committees, and the investigation and collection of information will be under their direction, and especially under the direction of the chairman of the committee. I may explain, as it will probably be of interest to hon. members, that the chairman of the committee on public health. is Mr. Osier, the chairman of the committee on forestry is-Senator Edwards, the chairman of the committee on waterways is Mr. Monk. Professor Robertson is chairman of the committee on lands and agriculture, and Mr. Has-zard, the premier of the province of Prince Edward Island is chairman of the committee on fisheries.
I do not quite understand the connection which makes it necessary for a conservation commission to have a committee on public health.

The work of that committee is largely connected with the pollution of streams, and the conservation of the public health generally. This was one of the subjects submitted at the Washington conference of last year, and I have no doubt whatever that there will be a very important work to be done in connection with that by the commission through this particular committee. The public health is regarded as one of the most important assets of the nation, and the work of the commission in this matter, it is expected, will be of great value.	.

To give practical and concrete instances, I may say that, so far, the commission has considered two questions in connection with public health, tuberculosis, and the pollution of rivers, and streams. It is our desire to collect all the information that can be collected in regard to the best method of bringing about the prevention of tuberculosis, and the best method of giving the assistance of the federal government to the bringing about of that end. When subjects have been thoroughly investigated, we make our Teport to the Governor in Council. Take also, for instance, the pollution of rivers and streams; that has come to a very serious point in Canada. The Senate has been investigating the matter. They have held a preliminary investigation, and brought in their reports, and have referred the report generally to our commission for further investigation, and that we may make a report on a practical method of dealing with it. I think I may say that the commission is well fitted to bring about an understanding between the provincial and the federal authorities, particularly in cases of jurisdiction over public health, the jurisdiction is concurrent by reason of the fact, that it comprises representatives from all the governments. There is a department that has some jurisdiction over public health under the administration of the Minister of Agriculture, and each province has a department of public health. But medical men say, and the fact- is clear, that there are gaps between the operation of the jurisdiction of the two bodies, and what they want is some complete plan agreed to by the provinces, and by the Dominion that will accomplish the purpose desired.

To the chairman of the commission.

The member for Brandon referred to the committee on fisheries of the conservation commission; perhaps he would give us a little inionnation with respect to the functions which that committee will perform. There is a committee of this House to look after matters pertaining to fisheries and marine, and it would be interesting for us to know what is the nature of the work which this branch of the conservation commission will take up, and to whom it will report.

, The committee on fisheries has not yet taken up their work or laid out their plans. I have no doubt that during the summer this committee will meet. The chairman of the committee is the premier of Prince Edward Island, and, he has been so. busily engaged in his administrative work that he has not been able to leave, and consequently there has been no meeting of the committee. My hon. friend asked to whom they would report. All the committees of the commission will report to the commission, and their reports will be embodied in the general report of the commission.

We have now a very elaborate Department of Fisheries which is divided up into a number of branches that are doing considerable work. We have also a committee of the House. Now, I cannot understand why another commission or committee should undertake to investigate matters which are now being investigated by a committee of this House. I sunpose there is at least an apparent need for the committee of this commission?

I cannot answer my hon. friend with any degree of definiteness. The idea was that by appointing that committee on fisheries we would make a careful examination of all the regulations relating to the preservation of fisheries throughout the Dominion, both by the Dominion and by the provinces; and if they found on careful examination of the regulations, and the principles on which they were enforced in the various provinces, that it would be in the public interest to make any recommendation for their amendment, they would do so. They have not yet made any examination.

It is strange that we should have this fisheries committee of the Conservation Commission when we have a standing committee of this House to deal with fisherv matters, summoning and obtaining evidence from all parts of the country. We are going to have another committee spending money in practically the same direction to get evidence in connection with the fisheries. 1 cannot see any necessity for a fisheries branch of the Conservation Commission. Are we going to appoint two committees to do practically the same work, or how are you going to separate the work of these committees? I protest against another committee being appointed by this parliament to waste the money of the country when w'e already

have a standing committee of this House, with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at its head, to look after the same interests. I do not see the need of appointing for the same purpose another committee which is a portion of this so-called Conservation Commission. If this Conservation Commission is going to do the whole business of this parliament we had better appoint it for that purpose. But we have already taken up that matter, we are dealing with it, and I see no good reason for appointing another committee, because there is no doubt that if the fisheries committee of the Conservation Commission is sent out to deal with fishery matters it will be a heavy charge upon this country. We do not desire to have that commission do work that is already provided for by this House.
I would like to ask the minister if the commission has been paid for the work it has already done, and how much it amounts to? [DOT]
I think the annual meeting cost about $1,600. I could not say how much has been paid in actual travelling expenses and how much in other expenses.
How many individuals drew that money?
There are thirty-two members of the commission, but, of course, a number of them were here, and they would not draw anything.
The law says that the commission shall consist of twenty members.
There are twelve ex-officio members besides, making thirty-two altogether, and, some of these being here already, they did not draw any travelling allowance.

It would be well that the two committees-the committee of this House and the committee of the Conservation Commission-should not proceed along similar lines, and that we should not take up the time of these different committees in doing the same work. I dare say there is work enough for both of them, but I think that the chairman of the commission should see to it that, the committee of the commission does not go over the same kind of work that the committee of the House is doing.

I think my hon. friend's suggestion is a very wise one. I am sure that the commission will find plenty of work to do without overlapping the work of the committee of this House. That would be far from their desire. My hon. friend from Brandon said a few minutes ago that one of the works that could be done by the Mr. CROSBY.
Fishery Committee was to find out exactly what are the various regulations, provincial and Dominion, with regard to fisheries, to see if at any place there was overlapping, or a break without any provision for proper care. A committee of this House cannot investigate provincial matters at all, but the commission being composed of representatives of the provinces, it is almost as much a provincial body as it is a Dominion body. The interests of the Dominion parliament, and of the provincial legislatures are all open to the investigation of this commission. Such work is not open to the investigation of a committee of this House. There is, therefore, an obvious possibility of the commission being able to do work which a committee of this House could hardly undertake.
Am I to understand that there is some doubt as to whether this parliament has the regulation of the fisheries?
I do not express any opinion.

If I understood the minister correctly, he stated distinctly that this committee could inquire into the rights of the provinces and of the Dominion in regard to the fisheries. The province has nothing to do with the fisheries of this country.
You are wrong.
They have not in the province from which I come.
They are owned by the provinces.
No, they are not.

By the old provinces.
Mr. CROSBY I am speaking of the only provinces that are worth speaking about in reference to this matter-the provinces on the Atlantic and the Pacific. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) stated that there was work for these two committees to do. I take issue with him there. There is no necessity for burdening this country with the expense of another committee, when we have a committee of this House to deal with the fisheries. It has cost this country a good deal for taking evidence and obtaining information in regard to the fisheries, and if this commission goes out and starts into the same thing we will be spending money which will not be well spent. I do not see the necessity for a Fisheries Committee working in conjunction with the Conservation Commission.
Mr. G0ODEVE. As representing the Minister of Public Lands in British Columbia I probably would be able, to a certain extent, to answer the question ask-

ed by hon. members. I feel that the question was amply justified and that they are entitled to the information asked for in regard to this particular committee of the Conservation Commission. Looking upon the fisheries as one of the great natural resources of thi3 country, and realizing that it is the object of this Conservation Commission, as far as possible, to conserve the natural resources, and get all the information available with regard to them, this committee was appointed in common with several other committees that have been referred to by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) as chairman of the commission. The work, as I understand it, of this committee, will be of a more general nature than the work which would be undertaken by a parliamentary committee, or a committee under the direction of the Department of Marine *nd Fisheries. It is to get a general id*a of the resources in fish of all parts of Canada, not only the information that they may get in connection with the fisheries of Canada but information in connection with the fisheries all over the world, information of rather broader nature than would be obtained by a committee of this House appointed to deal with the question of fisheries. The information that they would endeavour to collect would be on a broader and larger line. They might possibly act in an advisory capacity both to the Dominion government and the various provincial governments throughout Canada. If we get, for instance, statistical knowledge of my own province, and some other provinces as well, gathered together and reported to the general commission, I believe it would be very valuable to the provinces as well as to the Dominion in formulating policy. There has in the past been friction between the Dominion, and the province of British Columbia, as well as other provinces, and it is possible that an independent commission such as this might possibly get information which would enable these difficulties to be smoothed over and regulations framed which would be of advantage to the Dominion as a whole. As representing on the commission my own province I felt it my duty to state wThat I understood to be the prerogative of the commission.

In reference to the suggestion made by the hon, member (Mr. Armstrong) I would move as section 7 at the end of the Bill that the said Act be further amended by adding to it the following clauses which will make applicable Bill (No. 84) introduced by the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) to the officers of the commission, but which, according to the
understanding this afternoon, will not include the members of the commission.
I understood that the minister was to take clause (c) in sec-tipn 18, and add it to this Bill.

I may say that after the discussion the hon. member for Brandon had a short private conversation with the leader of the opposition, and he told me that that hon. gentleman had agreed with him that it would not be workable in that way, and therefore I left it out.
Then, I understand from the Minister of Agriculture that before the third reading of the Bill he and the hon. member for Brandon will get together and try to devise some clause to cover it?
I did not say that. I said that I hoped that before next session something might be worked out. I did not undertake to do it this session.

I do not suppose it is the purpose of the Minister of Agriculture to ask the House to pass the third reading of the Bill to-night. It had better be reprinted and held over for further consideration on account of these important amendments.
Certainly.

The purpose of this commission is a very laudable one, and we are all in sympathy with it; but why the servants of the commission should be penalized and the members of the commission left free from the operation of the Act I cannot see. .1 think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lambton should be accepted in toto, or the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Brandon might get together before the third reading and frame some compromise amendment that would meet the case. Am I right in saying that $50,000 is being appropriated for the purposes of this commission?
There is a vote of $15,000 in the main estimates, but I presume there will be a supplementary vote?
That is for employing engineers and other experts and collecting information.
Largely.
Is that information going to be available to the members of the House in the various committees and in the House itself?
It will be available to the public, I think?

The reason I ask that question is that in the Railway Committee

the other day a very important measure, the Bill proposed by the hon. member for Rainy River, was being considered, and one of the members of the committee moved that it be referred to the Conservation Commission for an opinion. The Minister of Public Works, who was present, resented the suggestion, stating that the committee would have to assume the responsibility of the Bill, although a Bill had been sent previously by the Private Bills Committee for a report from this commission. Is the expert knowledge of the commission on questions of this kind going to be available?
That question was fully discussed this afternoon.
If some means could be devised whereby we could get the benefit of the work and judgment of the commission during the session, I think it would be more valuable than their annual report.

The commission has only been in existence during the last fiscal year, which is just ended, and has not yet made its annual report. I have no hesitation in saying that we ought to be in a position to avail ourselves of any information which the commission gets, and the sooner that is published after it is acquired the better.
Should there not be a provision in the Bill enabling or requiring the commission to do that?

The hon. member for Brandon states that if the House wants any information from the commission on any subject, the commission would of course at any time obey an order of the House asking for anything of the kind; and, speaking for myself as a member of the commission, I have no doubt that the moment any information is acquired, in a form in which it could be published, the commission would not wait for its annual report to publish it, but would publish it perhaps in the form of a bulletin.

That is what wre have asked for time and again during this session.. We wanted a report from the commission on the Conmee Bill, but we were told that we had no right to demand or expect anything from them. I think there ought to be some statutory or parliamentary provision by which we w'ould be able to get the benefit of their knowledge at any time on any of these important questions if the House desired it. What the Minister of Agriculture says is, I think, in the right direction.

I think we shall have to consider a little the machinery by which that can be obtained, but I do not know that I can get it in such shape as to insert it in this Bill. It is a matter that requires Mr. S. SHARPE.
some consideraion as to the manner and method to be employed by the House or by the committees to get that information.

Why not amend clause 13 and say that the commission shall make its report to the Governor in Council at the end of the fiscal year or at any other time1 when requested to do so by the Governor in Council.

It seems to me that it is of considerable importance that we should be able to get information from the commission outside of the annual report. As I understand the members and officers of this commission will be making themselves familiar with questions concerning the conservation of the natural resources of Canada. Time and again this session in the Railway Committee a great many members have desired to get information that this commission might have had in their office, and I trust the minister will devise a means by which any committee of the House -wish-ins' information from the commission would get it at any time.

I certainly endorse the suggestion advanced by the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). It seems to me that as this commission goes on. they will become more expert and will gather around them a number of men expert in certain lines, who might be asked to furnish expert information on short notice, even although the commission might not have it at the time. Then, too, they would have a great deal of information on hand. A committee of the House might wish for information, and we could simply ask the commission and get a report immediately upon request,. It would be a great advantage to the House.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Siftonl is drafting an amendment.
I would suggest that the section read that they shall make their report at the end of the year or an interim report on any subject or subjects when requested by the Governor in Council.

The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) has drafted this amendment as an addition:
In addition to the annual report, the commission shall report from time to time to the Senate or to the House of Commons through the Speaker thereof whenever desired to do so by resolution of the Senate or of the House of Commons as may he.
By that method the information would be always available to either House.
Bill reported. '
