maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 187) to confirm and declare the rights of the Crown with re spect to water and water-power, and relating to the diversion, acquisition and use of water in the railway belt, in British Columbia-Mr. Oliver-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1; this Act may be cited as the Railway Belt Water Act

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: That means that it applies to no other locality than the railway belt? It does not apply to any other portion of the province or territory?

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: Will the minister explain the general purpose of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext:
Yes, the Bill, as was said a moment ago, and as implied by the title, affects what is called the railway belt of the province of British Columbia. But it affects also an area of three and a half million acres of land in. what is called the Peace river block. That is, it affects the whole of certain lands, which, under agreement between the province of British Columbia and the Dominion of Canada were granted by' the province to the Dominion in connection with the construction! of the Canadian Pacific railway. The administration of these lands thus rests upon the Dominion instead of upon the. province in which they were situated. During many years it was taken for granted that, while the land was administered by the Dominion, the wTater was controlled and administered by t.he province. Under that supposition, the general legislation of the province regarding water and water rights was applicable to
the railway belt, and grants were issued from time to time by the province of rights to water within the railway belt. While the right of the province was always assumed to exist in regard to water there was always a question as io whether it really did or did not exist, and so, in the case of some grants that were made by the provincial government, of rights to water within the railway belt, the grantees, in order to- make themselves secure, while they got the grant from the provincial government, got a quit claim from the Dominion government of any rights that the Dominion might possess. The_ question as to whether the right lay m the province or in the Dominion, however, was brought to an issue by a certain case at law which was begun some years ago, and in regard to which iudgment was given by the Exchequer Court in May, 1909. By the judgment of. the Exchequer Court, the water in the railway belt was vested in the Crown in the right of the. Dominion not in the right of the province. Of course the decision of the Exchequer Court was appealed, but it has since been upheld by the decision of the Supreme Court in Ottawa. It is, of course, to be expected that this decision will be again appealed and carried to the Privy Council. When the decision of the Privy Council is rendered, of course the matter will be considered settled^ and the right to the water will be considered finally vested either in the Dominion or in the province as the case may be. Inasmuch as rights to water in the railway belt had been issued by the province during a long period of years, and that at the end of that period the courts have declared that the rights did not rest with the province but with the Dominion the grants which had been given by the provincial government are grants without valid authority. Consequently, what may be called a chaotic condition exists in the railway belt in regard to water rights. Rights which were granted by the province have been invalidated by this decision of the courts, and as the Dominion has not undertaken to grant any rights, those who have held legal rights to the use of water for many years now find that their right to that water is subject to question at law. This is a condition which it is undesirable to continue. In everybody's interest, it is desirable that there should be a validating of existing rights.

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister think it the part, of wisdom to pass legislation for that purpose during the time when the question is before the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext:
Of course, if anything better can be done, it would be better not

to pass this legislation. But there are very large and important interests

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: That is the very reason why you should not disturb them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: We do not want to disturb them, but they are disturbed by the decision of the courts. What we want is to give them a legal standing, to carry their position forward at any rate until the final decision of the Privy Council has been given.

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: Is the Bill simply to validate, grants already issued by the province, or will it interfere with the case that is going before the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: It does not go further?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: No, it is not intended to interfere with any matter in litigation, that is, it is not intended to affect one way or the other any matter in litigation; but unless there is such legislation as this there is no basis for litigation.

maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: I do not like to ask this,, but not being a lawyer myself, and the member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) who went home for his Easter holidays and will be back to-night, and also the member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard), both lawyers, will be back to-night, I would suggest that the minister allow this Bill to stand until they arrive, for I am sure they would like to discuss it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext:
I have already arranged not to press the Bill through committee, but I was anxious to get it into committee, to explain its provisions in committee, and have it discussed in a preliminary way. Then I propose to leave it until those hon. gentlemen are present who are more deeply interested in the subject. As I was saying, we want to provide for a condition which exists for the time being. These rights which have been brought into a condition of uncertainty by the decision of the court, are of large financial importance, and it is not a sound policy that great interests should remain without legal standing, even for the space of a few months, when the authority of parliament is sufficient to cure that condition. One purpose of the Bill is to validate for the time being rights which were granted, but the foundation of which has been taken away by the decision of the court. The other purpose of the Bill is to enable the granting of new rights under the authority of the Dominion, so lcng as the authority rests in the Dominion, so that the development of water-power and water-rights in the belt will not be tied up or affected, pending a final decision of the Mr. OLIVER.
Privy Council. Briefly, the purpose of the Bill is to relieve a deadlock in the situation in regard to water-rights in the railway belt of the province of British Columbia, resulting from the decision of the court, and pending a final decision by the Privy Council.
Progress reported.

Mr. OLIVER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 163) to amend the Volunteer Bounty Act, 1908. He said: The Bill contains practically only one provision, it is a provision to allow the extension of one year for the location of bounty warrants, the issue of which was authorized under the Volunteer Bounty Act, 1908. Under that Act the location of bounty warrants was authorized up to the end of 1910. The Act was passed in 1908, and the rights under it expire at the end of 1910. As the persons who were entitled to this bounty were scattered all over the world, you might say, it was a considerable time before they all heard of the rights that had been accorded them under the Act. As it took a considerable time in some cases to establish their rights, it has been felt that the time allowed for the exercise of those rights was at least not more than enough to do justice to the case. At the same time it must be admitted that there was sufficient time if reasonable energy had been used on the part of all parties interested. On the other hand, there was this precedent which was present in the minds of many of those who were interested, that in no previous case had the right to bounties which were granted by parliament been terminated at the end of the first term of the grant. In the case of the volunteers of the first, second and third Red river expeditions, and in the case of the volunteers of 1885, the rights which were terminable on a certain date were extended from year to year by further Acts of parliament, and in every case there was a number of extensions, so that when the time given for location was so comparatively short and when the beneficiaries were so widely scattered it was felt that it was perhaps hardly fair, that, there having been such precedent for an extension of time, there should be no extension of time in this case.
Why do you not make it 1912 instead of 1911? There are only nine months until 1911. It is a very short time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The request was made by a number of volunteers for an extension of time until the end of 1912; that is a further extension of two years. Against that the view is taken that it is not sound policy to

allow this privilege for any longer time than is absolutely necessary, and we agreed to ask parliament for an extension of one year chiefly for the purpose of removing any claim of hardship that might possibly exist and yet give no longer time than was absolutely necessary to enable the grantees to get the full benefits of their grants.
What is the meaning of section 4?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For that reason the Bill asks merely for an extension of time for a period of one year. The amendment that I have spoken of is found in sections 2 and 3. Section 4 is a minor provision, and yet it is perhaps well that it should be ex^ plained. When the actual grant was issued, in some cases it was lost, and there is no provision for the re-issuing of any lost scrip. At the same time it is felt that if there had been an actual loss, the person who was entitled should not suffer if the loss could be proven in order to protect all interests. While the person who was entitled to this scrip was allowed to make entry for the amount of land that the scrip called for, before he was allowed to do so he was required to put up a bond with the department to the amount of $3,000 as security in case the scrip should actually turn up and its location be demanded by some person else. A guarantee company would charge a considerable amount of money as a consideration for putting up a bond of $3,000. It was felt that if we were going to extend the time for the location of this scrip, that is if we were going to lengthen the period during which this scrip shall be of value, that lengthening of the period was placing an added burden upon the person who had given the bond, so that instead of carrying the bond until the end of 1910 he would be compelled to carry it until the end of 1911, and we thought it was not fair that he should be required to carry the bond beyond the time for which the scrip was originally valid. So, by section 4 of the Act, we provide that in the specific cases in which the scrip has been lost and a bond has been put up with the department, the particular scrips mentioned in the schedule on the back of the Bill are not valid after the end of 1910. The provision in section 5 is to get over a flaw which occurred in the drafting of the Act passed in 1908 by which there was a contradiction in terms. While the Bill declared that the rights should only be in accordance with the Homestead Act, there was certain wording which seemed to indicate that the right oi locating under the Act did not require to be exercised until the end of the year 1910. As there was a contradiction in terms of the Act the department administered it in accordance with what was believed to be sound public policy, and in accordance with 203 ,
the intent of parliament. Therefore, it was administered in accordance with the terms of the Homestead Act. Occupancy of the land was insisted upon within six months after the date of entry. Under an order in council, before the scrip was granted an agreement was signed by the grantee that he would conform to that requirement, and section 5 of this Act is- for the purpose of validating that order in council. These are the three provisions of the Bill, one of major importance, extending the time for location of the scrip for one year until the end of 1911, the other two of minor importance, one arising out of the administration, providing for certain accidents which have occurred, and the third curing an error in the wording of the original Act.

May I ask the minister how many volunteers have taken advantage of the bounty, and how many it is expected will take advantage of it before its expiration? I may say that there is some criticism in the press, and some circulars have been issued, stating that this extension of time is more in the interest of the speculator in this land than in that of the volunteer. No doubt all this information has been communicated to the minister. Perhaps he would be good enough to state to the committee whether, in his opinion, this extension is more in the interest of the volunteer or the speculator?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The answer depends on how many of these grants still remain to the benefit of the volunteer and how many have passed out of his hands into the hands of the speculator. If more than half are in the hands of the speculator the extension will certainly benefit the speculator more than the volunteers. If some are still in the hands of the volunteers it will certainly benefit the volunteers more than the speculators. However, that was not a feature of the case that was considered. The desire was that the volunteer should receive the full benefit that it was intended he should receive, and if he retains his scrip, whether he was in the majority or in the minority, our desire was that he should get the full benefit. That was the case that was pressed upon us by the representatives of the volunteers that called upon the government. In the original Bill the principle was accepted by the House that the person who acquired the scrip from the volunteer should stand in exactly the same position as to his rights as the volunteer himself. It. was the interest of the volunteer that it should be so, it was the will of parliament it should be so, and parliament having so decided in the interest of the volunteer the government in preparing the Bill did not draw any distinction between the scrip, which was still in the hands of the volunteers, and the scrip



which had passed out of their hands into the hands of speculators.

When the Bill was introduced I drew the attention of the minister to that aspect of the case. These young volunteers had almost given up hope of getting scrip, because year after year excuse was given by the government: first they were not sure whether they would retain control of the Dominion lands when the provinces were established, and having retained control the government for years hesitated before they issued the scrip. Had the volunteers known when they returned from South Africa in 1900 to 1902, that the scrip would be issued in 1908, or had it been known in 1908 that they would have had until 1910 to settle on the homesteads, they would have laid up some money to enable them to make a start. But, they were only given to the end of 1910 when the scrip was issued, and many of them being unable to raise the necessary funds to go to their homesteads by that date, they sold their scrip at a sacrifice to these dealers all over the country, who like all other dealers, were some of them honest and some most unscrupulous. A number of these volunteers were practically swindled out of this scrip by these dealers. It would be a scandal to give these speculators the advantage of this extension of time provided for in the Bill. If any advantage is to accrue to any one it should accrue to the volunteer who sold this scrip. The volunteer who is not yet located should get two years extension, but the speculator should not be entitled to any advantage. He beat the volunteers -why in this very city one of these speculators got a young man to sell him the scrip for $10, and the Minister of Militia took the precaution to get the Minister of the Interior to provide in the Act that any agreement for the sale of the scrip before it was issued should be cancelled. That was done to protect the volunteers. It is very easy to provide that the speculator shall not get this advantage by adding a clause to that effect to the Bill. There is another aspect of the case to which I wish to call attention. Unfortunately two or three of these young fellows died on the way to South Africa, and in the case of one who died in the Gulf of the St. Lawrence, his friends received the scrip, but it was refused to the friends of others, the excuse being given that in the first place the scrip was issued without understanding the technicalities of the law. I hold that as the minister granted the scrip in one case he is in duty bound to do it in the others, and if the law does not permit him to, he should have the law changed. I also maintain that the men who enlisted and went to Halifax, and through accident or illness were prevented from going to the seat of war, are entitled to the scrip. Then again, Mr. OLIVER.
I cannot understand why the civil surgeons did not get scrip. In the first place I do not know why the civil surgeons were not enrolled, because in the columns I had anything to do with they were all enrolled. However, in many localities, the civil surgeons remained civil surgeons to the end of the war. But, they were in the thick of the fight, and they are, in my opinion, absolutely entitled to scrip. Again, I say to the minister, that it would be a scandal to give this extension of time to the speculator, who practically got the scrip for nothing from the volunteers. I know two or three cases where the boys borrowed money and went out to settle, but in other cases they were not so fortunate, and were obliged to sell the scrip at whatever was considered to be the market value. Again I say that the speculators should not be allowed to still further profit at the expense of the volunteers.

I hold that the men who garrisoned the city of Halifax before any volunteers were sent out to South Africa from Canada, and who took the place of the Imperial troops to allow them to go to South Africa, are entitled to scrip. These men enlisted as soldiers of the King and they could be sent to South Africa at any moment, and are entitled to consideration. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister last ye'ar, and I hope that tonight he will be able to tell us that the men who garrisoned Halifax will get their scrip the same as the others.

Some time ago the minister told me that he was considering whether he would open a portion of the railway belt for location under this scrip. I would be glad to know if he has yet reached a decision on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Nothing has been done in that direction. Provision is not made in either the Bounty Act, or the Dominion Lands Act for location within the railway belt, and I hardly think that it would be in the interest of settlement in the railway belt that such a provision should be made. There are some 7,000 of these grants which call for 320 acres of land each, and it seems to me that the injury, may I say, that is done on the prairies, where the land exists in millions of acres, is so serious from the establishment of this number of special grants, that if it were transferred to the limited area of the railway belt of British Columbia, I am afraid that it would tend against the development of the railway belt to a degree that would be very injurious to the interests of the province. I shall be quite prepared to discuss the matter at a later date, though I may say that it is not involved in any way in this Bill.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he did not give out the statement last year, when this House was in session, that there would be no extension of time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not that I have any remembrance of. .

I regret that the minister has such a short memory. I would like further to know what reasons there are at the present time for extending the time. I object to that, at any rate with regard to scrip held by speculators. I think it is wrong in every sense of the word. I believe it is entirely justifiable that the men who went to South Africa and took their chances for the sake of the old flag, should be allowed all the opportunity possible to take advantage of the concession granted them by the government; but the speculators, as everybody knows, a3 the minister himself knows, bought the rights from these volunteers for a nominal sum; and I think it is a shame to enable these men to enrich themselves at the expense of the volunteers, and of this country by changing the law in this way. I know of my own knowledge that no later than January last a certain speculator of Winnipeg, representing the old grafting bunch there, came to Ottawa, interviewed this government, and then telegraphed to a broker in Winnipeg: Buy up all the scrip you can, at whatever price you can get it.' Scrip was bought at $750-320 acres of land for less than $2.50 an acre. I strongly object to that sort of thing, not because I happen to be on one side of the House, and my hon. friend on the other side, but I object to it as a matter of right and wrong. Protect the volunteers, and the people of Canada, but do not play into the hands of speculators. As I do not wish to detain the House, I will leave whatever other remarks I have to make until we go into Committee of the Whole on the Bill.

I would like to say a word on behalf of those volunteers who lost their lives at sea on the way to South Africa. In Hamilton there are two widows whose sons, the only support they had volunteered and started for South Africa. One of them died on the way, and was buried at sea; the other died after he had landed in South Africa, and was buried there. These widows I know to be very much in need of support, and this grant would be of very great assistance tojhem. When the Act was passed I do not believe it was the intention to leave out those volunteers who died at sea. I have spoken to some of the ministers on the subject, and they have practically admitted that it was a mistake to put through the Act in 203*
that form. I appeal to the minister to take into consideration these cases. There is no good argument why the grant should not be made to those who died at sea; they practically did as much as those who went to South Africa, and fought and came back. I do not think anybody will object to this, as it is only fair, and I would like the minister to add a clause to the Bill providing for cases of this kind.

Few of us, especially from the west, have not received letters, and petitions from public bodies, and individuals opposing this Bill. Grain Growers' Associations all through Manitoba have passed resolutions condemnatory of such an extension of time. The Grain Growers' ' Guide,' the official organ of the grain growers of Manitoba, contains the following strong article condemning Ithe extension of time as a crowd of speculators will be the beneficiaries. The article is as follows:
Hon. Frank Oliver has introduced a Bill into the House of Commons to extend the time for settlement duties to begin on South African scrip until the end of 1911. This action is taken by Mr. Oliver despite the vigorous protests made by western farmers' associations. He knows that the scrip is now held by speculators and that his Bill will simply be a means of robbing western farmers still further. It is hard to understand how Mr. Oliver, with his eyes wide open, can take the part of the land grabbers against the bona fide farmers of the west. It begins to look as though the interests of the people were regarded very lightly at Ottawa. At the rate things are going a farmer will have to contribute more largely than ever to the support of the wealthy and privileged classes. Mr. Oliver is Minister of the Interior and is supposed to be looking after the interests of the settlers in the west. Instead of that he seems to be promoting legislation in the interests of the land grabbers.
This is a pointed and strong expression, no doubt elicited by the fact that these protests must have been sent to the Minister of the Interior, and his department, and apparently no attention has been paid to them. The principal reason advanced by the minister is that a precedent has been established in other land grants. I am not conversant with the conditions of other land grants, but present day conditions cannot be compared with conditions when the other grants were made. Immigrants are coming in by thousands; in a few years we will have little good land left for free homesteading purposes, and the speculators will utilize the scrips for their own aggrandisement, and to the disadvantage of the bona fide settler. It has been argued that if an extension of time is refused, all the grants will be placed on the market at the same time, causing a fall in price. If you discriminate, and allow the extension

only to the veterans who hold their land this will be obviated, whereas if there is an extension to include all grants, the prices will be enhanced, and the speculators will be the beneficiaries. I have seen it stated in a Winnipeg paper that since the Bill was introduced there has been a rise in the value of these land grants, and if the Bill passes there will be a further rise. At a meeting of the Grain Growers' Association at Shoal lake the other day a resolution was about to be put against the granting of an extension of time, but a prominent friend of gentlemen opposite asked the meeting not to pass the resolution saying it would not be necessary, because they had the assurance of the Prime Minister that no extension would he granted. By reason of that statement the resolution was not passed. I will not say such a promise was made, but that information, wherever obtained, was the means of heading off that resolution. We object to the speculator being the chief beneficiary as he would be if the Bill passed in its present form.
In what way would it rob the farmers of the west if this extension were made?

Some of the farmers are themselves desirous of getting the scrip as bona fide settlers, and if this Bill passes the price will be so enhanced that it will be beyond their reach. The speculator will not settle on the land, hut many farmers would like to get the lands, and this will put them beyond their reach.
Would they not he speculators if they did?
No, they would settle on the lands or purchase them for their sons.
If I had scrip I would have to place somebody on the land.
If the hon. gentleman was trafficking in this it would not be either to locate some one or to settle there himself.
Suppose I were.
You can suppose whatever you like, but the ordinary speculator is not putting any one on the land.
Men whom I know who have bought scrip have put people on the land.

There are two sides to the question, and the pressure has not all been from the speculator. I know of two cases in Wentworth of people who were unable to accumulate a sufficient fund to settle on the land, and who would be obliged to sell out at a very small price if they could not have an extension until they could accumulate a sufficient fund to go on the land.
We have no objection to that.

I fancy that a quite large percentage of the urgency for this extension has come from that source, and so far as I know none has come from the speculative side of the question. I think the minister's action is to meet the case largely of the genuine volunteer who has not been able so far to accumulate enough to settle. I think the speculative class is small compared to the bona fide volunteer who wishes to settle.

I am not interested in scrip, I have never bought any because I have never had the money to buy it, but at the same time I know a number of young men who have scrip who have not sold it to speculators, but would be willing to sell it for a satisfactory price. If the extension would enhance the value the probabilities are that the original holder would also benefit as much as the so-called speculator. A few men from our section went to South Africa, and I do not know of any case where they were in any way defrauded about their scrip. A good many in my opinion got full value for their scrip, and the men who bought the scrip have not been able to get men to go on the land and locate for them. I know that they have been endeavouring, some of them very earnestly, to get men to go out and locate on the land. They personally do not want to go. For my part, I am not so much down on the so-called speculator. There is a speculation in everything we do, if we apply it in that way. I think there is nobody here who would not be ready to buy a lot in the city of Ottawa and sell it for an advance in price. I do not see why the man who bought this land from the young man who refused to locate on it should not have the same opportunity to get even with the money he has expended as anybody else. There is too much agitation against so-called speculation, but I do not know any gentlemen who are not perfectly willing to take an advance in price on anything they happen to buy, from a steer to a farm.

There are, as my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said, two sides to this question. Hon. members on the other side should remember that when the Act was passed, everybody in the House and country contemplated that a very large number of young men who went to South Africa, would not go to the Northwest to settle. Indeed, many hon. members -would not have supported the Bill if they had thought that many of these men would remove from the places in which they resided. It was expected that a large number of these young men in the east would dispose of their rights and receive the money. I was one of those

who pressed upon the minister the importance of extending the time, and I spoke particularly on behalf of at least four young men in my own country entitled to receive this scrip, who had not made the location and were not in a position to get a title. 1 say that these young men had a perfect right to have this extension given.
We all agree with you.

But there is no good in agreeing that there shall be an extension," and at the same time preventing the sale of the scrip at a figure that will give the owner as much as he ought to get out of it. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) made it clear that his object is to lessen the value of the scrip in the hands of the bona fide veterans. I do not think that the House will agree with that. It may be that some gentlemen in the west would prefer to get this land cheaper than, it would be possible to get it with the whole Dominion in competition for it, including the bona fide speculator, as the hon. member for North Oxford has said I think the men to be first considered are the boys who went to South Africa, and I think the solution of this whole thing is to keep in mind the idea that they should get as much out of it as they can. I think there can be no reasonable objection to the extension. Some of these young men waited, thinking that they could go out, thinking that home conditions would permit of their going. I think it would be unreasonable to say that no extension shall tie given, and still more unreasonable to give the extension, and at the same time impair the value of the scrip.

I agree that we should not do anything to impair the value of the scrip in the hands of the volunteer, who originally got it, and whom parliament intended should be benefited. But, if I understood the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hnghes), his proposition was to deny the benefits of this Bill to scrip bought by people for speculative purposes before the passing of this Bill. And in that I agree with him. In answer to the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), I would point out that, with regard to scrip already sold, the volunteer got the value of that scrip with its standing restrictions and limitations. If that scrip had been good for an additional .year, it would have been worth more money to the man who bought it-he -would have had larger opportunity. But the volunteer got just what it was worth as scrip giving the limited right to locate before the end of 1910. Now, this measure is going to add value to that, scrip by giving this extension of a year. That value ought to go to the volunteer who holds his scrip and wants to sell it. The day after this Bill is passed,
he ought to be able to sell it on the basis of the extended time. But I do not see why we should allow legislation to give to the man who bought the scrip for speculative purposes a greater value than he bought, none of that added value inuring in any way to the benefit of the man who sold it. If the volunteer had known that the time was going to be extended for a year, he could have sold his scrip at a higher figure. The country is- coming now to the rescue of the .man who bought the scrip with the knowledge that the period for location would run out at the end of this year, and paid a price accordingly. We are going to make him a present of an advanced value that will not benefit the volunteer. It would not be a difficult thing to make the amendment suggested. There is a section in the Act restricting its application with regard to particular cases mentioned in the schedule. The amendment could be made by introducing into the fourth section after the word * Act ' in the second line these words:
Or any bounty certificate that has been, prior to the passing of this Act, sold or transferred to any person acquiring the same for purposes of speculation or re-sale.
This would simply except cases where parties have bought this scrip as terminable at the end of the year. The expression ' for purposes of speculation or resale ' are introduced so as to make the exception inapplicable in case the volunteer has given his scrip to his children, or to a relative gratuitously. The holder of the scrip in such a case ought not to be prevented from getting all that is coming to him. But I do not think we ought to legislate in such a way as to give the speculator more than he bought and paid for.

I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member from Hamilton (Mr. Stewart), and the two cases of real hardship that he mentioned. These cases are ones for which, unfortunately, provision was not made in the original Bill. And, as the Bill before us simply provides for an extension of the time under the Act, for locating the scrip, such cases as the hon. member referred to cannot be taken into account at this time. With regard to the application of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby), he seems ts ask on behalf of men who remained in Halifax while others went out to fight the battles of the empire in South Africa. There was a point made by the-hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) with Tespect to the value of the scrip that was being sold, and he seemed to convey the idea that it was being sold for $2 per acre, and that carried the right to get 320 acres. I understand that the South African Volunteer Bounty Act carries the

right to locate 320 acres, but the man who locates it must go and perform homestead duty on the land. Now I am in favour of the Bill for the reason that there has been, particularly throughout the country from which I come, a general sentiment during the'past year that the time for the location of South African scrip would be extended. To draw a distinction between men who are holding scrip for speculative purposes', and men who will actually locate on the land, and live on it, and perform their residence duties, I think is impossible. I know a number of men who live near the city of Regina, farmers who have already homesteaded there, and who have bought that scrip for the purpose of locating, and going actually on the land. If a man does not locate on it before the end of this year, he would come under the head of what some hon. gentlemen are pleased to call speculators. I submit that those farmers who have bought that scrip honestly in open market are just as much entitled to consideration as the men who were original holders, and are still holding the scrip. Like the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), I have seen the resolution passed by the Western Grain Growers, though I have not had any representations made by them to me in opposition to the Bill as proposed. I have only had one letter protesting against an extension of time proposed in the Bill. It is quite true that the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' convention at Prince Albert did pass a resolution opposing an extension of time on the ground that the scrip had gradually drifted into the hands of speculators. I must say that I know in my vicinity some men who have bought scrip, and are holding it for speculative purposes, but they bought the scrip honourably in open market, and I do not see why they should not be entitled to consideration. I have had representations made to me asking for an extension of time. There is a South African volunteer association of Canada which sent out petitions for an extension of time, not to the end of 1911, but to the end of 1912. They do not ask that they alone be granted an extension of time, they do not ask that speculators be excepted from the Bill, but they ask for an extension of time generally. I have before me a copy of the petition, and one of the arguments used in it appears to be a very reasonable one. It says:
Unless the time is extended a premium will foe put upon speculation, and instead of the volunteer reaping the benefit of the grant he will foe forced in every case where he cannot arrange to make entry during the year 1909 to sacrifice his right and assign it for whatever unay foe offered at a time when the speculator in scrip is able to force a sale at a depreciation.

It seems to me there is considerable force in that argument, which is used by the volunteers themselves. If they do not get an extension they will be forced to sell their scrip at a depreciated value, because many of these men are not in a position to perform their settlement duties.

If the case mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton is correct, a great injury would be done to_ these two men. He states that two families have lost a son each. Now, those men were passed by the doctor as good, healthy men, they started on the trip to South Africa, but Providene did not permit them to get there, and they died at sea. I think those men are just as much entitled to scrip as any man who arrived there and fought on the battlefield. They went there for the purpose of doing their duty, and had they arrived there no doubt they would have done their duty. I think a great injury will be done to the families of those two men if scrip is not granted to them. I look upon those two men as just as deserving as any men who were shot on the battlefields. If scrip is not granted to those two families more injury will be done to them than by extending the time in favour of any other persons. I hope tfte minister will take these two cases into his favourable consideration.

I hope when the Bill reaches the committee stage that the minister will favourably consider the extension of these privileges to those men who enlisted and left their homes for the purpose of going to South Africa, but who, through accident or illness, became invalided. I think their legal representatives or nearest of kin should be entitled to the same consideration as those wrho served in South Africa and returned. In particular, I think that any man who enlisted in a regular way, who started out to perform his duties, who loyally obeyed orders, and was injured while doing his duty, should receive all the benefits of the Act. I think there are only a few cases of that kind, probably not more than a dozen, in the whole of Canada. I have only heard of two or three cases of that kind, and I hope the minister will consider them favourably.
Is this the last extension there will be of this Volunteer Bounty Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that question. There is no extension yet, nor will there be an extension unless parliament should agree to the Bill which I now present to it. If my hon. friend wants my own view, I would say, certainly not, I would not think favourably of any further extension.

I think this Bill is rather unfair to a certain number of men who had to sell their scrip, and who had no knowledge that the time was going to be extended, while some others held on to it. I think the minister .should say definitely now whether this is the last extension or not. It is only fair that the man who holds scrip now should know whether this is the last extension. The government must have some knowledge of that, and they should say now what their intention is.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and" House went into committee thereon.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We propose in the morning to take concurrence on the re-maiijing items of the supplementary estimates for the year just closed, including the special Supply Bill, and confined entirely to those items. That, I expect, will only take a short time, and after that, the Race Track Bill, I understand, will have precedence.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Wednesday, April 6, 1910.
